subtopic: MEETING OF GENERAL ASSEMBLY IN NEW YORK- CANADIAN DELEGATION

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, as the house has already been informed, the second part of the first session of the general assembly of the united nations has been summoned to open in New York on, September 23. Under the charter, member states are entitled to be represented in the general assembly by five delegates. The assembly will have before it a long and complicated agenda, and this will necessitate the appointment of a fairly large Canadian delegation. I am now able to inform the house of those who have been invited to serve as delegates and as alternate delegates. The names of the advisers will be announced later.
The five delegates will be myself, as chairman of the delegation; the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin), and the minister without portfolio, Senator Robertson. I am happy to say that the leaders of the Progressive Conservative party and of the C.C.F., the hon. members for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken) and Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), have also accepted the invitation to serve as delegates.
The following gentlemen have been invited to serve as alternate delegates:	The leader
of the opposition in the senate, Hon. J. T. Haig; the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mellraith), who is the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply; together with, from the public service, Mr. Hume Wrong, the Associate Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs; Mr. M. W. Mackenzie, Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, and Mr. H. L. Keenleyside, Canadian Ambassador to Mexico.
The advisers to the delegation will be selected from those in the public service with special competence in the matters that are expected to come before the assembly.

subtopic: LABOUR PROGRESSIVE PARTY-RADIO TALKS OVER THE NATIONAL NETWORK

speechtext: On the 'orders of the day:

subtopic: LABOUR PROGRESSIVE PARTY-RADIO TALKS OVER THE NATIONAL NETWORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Right Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). According to press reports, Tim Buck, leader of the Labour Progressive party, and Guy Caron, another well-known communist, are scheduled to talk to-morrow evening over the C.B.C. In view of the findings of the report on espionage activities and the charges levelled against the Labour Progressive party, is it the minister's intention to intervene and prevent this communist propaganda over the C.B.C.?
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) (Text): The hon. member asks if the Minister of Justice is going to intervene to prevent certain people from speaking over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I must say to the hon. member that the Minister of Justice has no right to do that under the statute which governs the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and which was passed by this parliament. There is before parliament at the present time a bill to amend that statute. If parliament deals with that bill it will be the privilege of any hon. member to propose any amendment that he sees fit to that bill to give other controls over the broadcasting facilities than those which are provided in accordance with the statute. Until that is done the Minister of Justice has no greater right to give direction to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation than has the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond).

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON

speechtext: Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair there is a matter I should like to draw to the attention of the house, and a request I should like to make to the government on behalf of the constituents whom I have the honour to represent. The fact is that the people of Winnipeg North Centre are not alone in their concern about this matter. I refer to announcement which has been made by the government to the effect that the milk subsidy is to be removed, with the result that an increase in the price of milk to consumers may take place very shortly.
It is well-established that one of the most nutritious foods needed by our people is milk.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: And still the cheapest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
Canada's food rules as approved by the council of nutrition in 1944, contained in a report on nutrition and the production and distribution of food published this year under the authority of the minister of national health and welfare (Mr. Claxton), lists the desirability of a sufficient quantity of milk as the first of these food rules. Accordingly, the possibility of an increase in the price of milk to 14, 14J or 15 cents a quart is a matter of very serious concern to all Canadian people. It is of particular concern to urban dwellers in a constituency such as mine.
The matter is not only of concern to the consumer; it is also of concern to the producer. A person engaged in the production of so vital a commodity as milk certainly should have his return from that effort guaranteed, and he should not be subject to losses such as are bound to result if the price of milk goes up and the purchase of milk is therefore reduced. I was interested in reading in the Toronto Globe and Mail this morning a news dispatch from Ottawa which reads in part as follows: it is under the by-line of Kenneth Cragg:
Ottawa, August 26.-Government decision, announced to parliament last Thursday, not to continue producer subsidies on whole milk after October 1, was taken contrary to the recom-tnemlation of agriculture minister Gardiner.
Mr. Gardiner, it was learned to-day, when he left for Europe, left behind for his colleagues advice for a compromise on subsidy policy, in view of^ labour's wage demands and the government's determination to support price control.
The article goes on to suggest that, although the Minister of Agriculture is not rated as an authority on finance or labour, he had something very strong to say about this matter in relation to prices:

Milk Subsidy
He argued that an increase now in milk price, which affects the consumer faster than an increase in almost any other food product, would be the worst possible timing.
I am not going to take time at the moment to comment on this division in the cabinet, similar to some other divisions which we have noted of late, but I do suggest that in this instance the minister is right in protesting against any change in policy which results in an increase in the price of milk.
I could go on, but the case is so strong that it is not necessary to add to it. I simply rise to register my strongest protest at this move being taken at this time, and I earnestly hope that the government will reconsider its policy and see to it that the price of milk does not go up any further; in fact in my view it should be restored to the ten cent ceiling that we had during the course of the war.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having been a milk producer for twenty-five years I feel I should say something on this matter, because the situation which is facing Canada to-day is a- serious one. We have had an increase of four cents in six months. The consumer subsidy of two cents has been removed, which means that the consumer has to pay 12 or 12J cents, according to the city he lives in; and now, if the producer subsidy is taken off, as the government intends to do on October 1, the man who is getting his milk for ten cents will have to pay 14J or 15 cents. I suggested in the house some considerable time ago that if the government had done this sort of thing to half the extent, that is if it had taken one cent off, it would have been better. We all know that these subsidies have to come off, and we have to get back to a pre-war basis. But on the one hand the government refuses to give increased wages to the man who is going to purchase the milk, and on the other hand the cost of producing milk is going up by leaps and bounds.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: What about the family allowances?

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: My hon. friend will make his speech after I have done, and I shall be delighted to listen to him.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: Will you? Thanks.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: In answer to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) I might tell him that we had family allowances when we were getting these subsidies.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: Only for one year.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
Until such time as we get back to normal conditions these things will have to be looked after, and if they are not looked after by the government, who is going to look after them?
To-day the cost of producing milk is going up. People who have followed that occupation all their lives just cannot make ends meet, because men are getting wages on the farms such as they never got before. Those increased wages have to be paid, because men can get fine jobs in industry to-day, where they do not have to work fourteen hours a day, as they do on the farm, so the farmer has to pay them high wages to get them to produce milk.
There is a scarcity of fodder in the western provinces. That may seem unbelievable, but it is true. I have been out there and have seen the condition myself. If the fifty-five cents producer subsidy is taken off, the price of milk will rise to 14*1 cents. I think the government acted very unfairly in this matter. The wartime prices and trade board set the price of milk during the war, and now that the war is over and we are getting back to normal they throw the whole thing into the lap of the provincial milk boards. I asked the Minister of Agriculture a question about this, and he told me that they wanted it that way. I do not know whether it is so, but certainly the situation is a serious one and the government must face it. They have either to reinstate a part of these subsidies or make some other arrangement. As I have said before, milk is not only a drink; it is also a food, and if we want to build a healthy Canada we must see to' it that the people get milk. In the Winnipeg area there are 1,000 shippers sending in milk now, whereas before the war there were only 600. The reason is that the big fellows are going out of business and it is only the man who is producing two or three cans of milk a day, who is able to exploit his children by getting them to milk the cows before they go to school and when they come home in the evening, who is producing milk. We shall never have a healthy situation so long as the milk producers are not enabled to stand on their feet.
I do not wish to take up a lot of time but I appeal to the member of the government, whoever it is that represents the Minister of Agriculture, and also to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, to do something about this and do it right away because, as I say, the situation is serious.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
I am prompted to say a word or two on this subject by an editorial which appeared in my local
Milk Subsidy

newspaper a couple of days ago, recapitulating the demands of the people of my particular city for the continuance of the milk subsidies. 1 do not think it is necessary for me to say, nor does anyone else need to say, that milk is a highly nutritious food, and it is important that there should be an adequate supply of it, particularly at this time when our children are returning to school. The ration of this commodity should not be reduced.
Some time ago I appealed through the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, and through him to the wartime prices and trade board, for a permit for a certain organization in my home town of Saskatoon. It is a newly organized cooperative store which has been in operation seven or eight months and in that time it has accumulated to itself seven or eight hundred families as customers. I appealed to the minister to try to get a quota of canned milk for that cooperative store. I do not think that the distribution of .quotas for canned milk in Saskatoon is at the moment equitable, because this particular *cooperative canno-t get a tin of canned milk. I know there are reasons for that, but in the light, of what has happened now, and in view *of the fact that the subsidy is to be withdrawn, I would ask the minister if he thinks it is right that these people, who cannot procure canned milk, are also to be denied a supply of fresh milk because of the increased price in the commodity itself.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
I
know that everyone wants to go home, but I must tell the house that every member here is precisely in my position-elected to do a certain job for his constituents and for the people of Canada. I will not discuss the question of a milk subsidy either as a producer of milk, because I am not one, or as a large consumer, since my family is grown up; but I will speak from information given me by a very important Canadian organization, the local council of women, the members of which make a particular job of studying the needs of less fortunate people in their communities. They are earnest, sincere citizens. I will not take time to put on the record a number of letters I have received from various councils of this organization but I would say that they are earnestly, desperately and sincerely concerned over the welfare of the children of the larger and less fortunate families in the areas from which they write me.
The government would be well advised to reconsider the whole matter and to continue the subsidies until the transition from wartime and semi-inflation or complete inflation, or
IMr. Knight.]
whatever it is we have at the present time, is completed and things are properly organized. There are many children who will not have their full ration of milk this winter if the subsidy is taken off now. I am not trying to be critical. I know the trouble the government is having. I know the members of the government are doing the best they can in the light of the information they have and from their view of the situation, but I do believe they would do well to give the matter further consideration and continue the subsidies until such time as plentiful supplies of milk are on the market. If they do not, I know something of the producer and of milk production, and I know, as the hon. member for Selkirk says, that a great many people now in the business of producing milk will gradually get rid of their dairy herds, or some of them, reduce them to the point where they can handle the business with family labour. If they have to buy a lot of feed from outside, and hire outside labour, undoubtedly they will feel that the game is not worth all the work and expense and risk involved, and they will reduce their herds to the point where the risk is lowest and where they can handle the business with available labour in the family. In that event supplies of milk will be less than they are at the present time.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
I concur entirely in what the other speakers have said in this regard. Three weeks or a month ago I wrote to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture asking them to continue the subsidies. I am like these other gentlemen in that I was brought up on a farm and I know what the milk producers have to go through in producing milk. At the present time, with the clamour for high, wages, it is impossible for the farmers to produce milk more cheaply than they are doing it now. Not only is the welfare of our children at stake; the welfare of the future population of Canada is involved1 if we do not provide the people now with the nutrition they need. I would therefore urge the government to reconsider their decision, if they have decided not to continue the subsidy because this is no time to have our children go without this valuable food.
There are very few members of this house, I would say there are no more than forty, who know what a farmer has to go through in order to produce milk, and if the majority of hon. members apart from those forty were on farms trying to produce milk themselves they would understand the difficulties of the dairy farmer. Again I urge the government to reconsider the decision.

Milk Subsidy

speakeroldname: Mr. R. W. MAYHEW (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: I will not attempt to answer the various arguments that have been advanced. In a matter of a day or two the estimates of the wartime prices and trade board will be up for discussion and there will be no reason why this question could not be discussed at that time, when I can make necessary answers. In the meantime I will point out that the handling of milk has been turned back to the milk boards of the provinces, and whether they want an increase or not is something that is up to them.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) on the contribution which he has made to this important discussion. The views which he has expressed represent the opinions of hon. members in all sections of the house. The statement made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mayhew) is not very helpful. If we are to continue the wartime prices and trade board it is important that subsidies in connection with the production of milk be maintained. If something is not done in the next six months there will be an increase in that six months period of from ten to fifteen cents a quart in some parts of Canada. It is obvious that with the general increase in the cost of living, old age pensioners and people in the lower income brackets will find it impossible to obtain a sufficient quantity of milk at the high prices.
There has been little criticism of the subsidy policy carried out by' the government during the war. This is no field in which the wartime prices and trade board should retreat and throw the matter back on the lap of the provincial authorities. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton:
That all the words after the word "that'' to the end of the question be left out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house desires to record its opinion that consideration should be given to the continuance of the milk subsidy so as to ensure adequate return to milk producers and make possible the consumption of milk for the nutrition of the Canadian people without any further increase in the price thereof to the consumers."
I should like to draw Your Honour's attention to the decisions of former Speakers as recorded in Beauehesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms at page 529. In 1912 the Hon. James S. Sproule ruled that:
Private members may introduce resolutions which do not directly involve the expenditure of public money but simply express an abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant.
Then in a relative paragraph on the next page we find the following:
As this is a question not always understood, it may be explained that such resolutions, being framed in general terms, do not bind the house to future legislation on the subject, and are merely intended to point out to the government the importance and necessity of such expenditure.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
This milk question is of great interest to the house and Canada. The government could very well shorten the discussion by themselves giving us a little milk in the form of a word as to what their intentions are. The government have been particularly silent on the question. The people of the country who may have to suffer because of the lack of subsidy would not mind doing so if there was good reason for it. If the government have a good reason for doing this, let them say so now and we should all be ready' to listen to reason.
That is all I wish to say. There is no use labouring the point, but we ought to have some real reply from the government as to why they still persist in the policy of withdrawing subsidies.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
I do not want to take up much time; I want to say something but I still want to go home. Therefore I say that I concur in the remarks which have been made so far.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): I favour the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). Having been a dairyman myself I know something of the difficulties of dairymen; I know something about the cost of production and the difficulties which people have in obtaining sufficient milk for the proper nutrition of their families. It is significant to note that prior to the introduction of the federal subsidies on milk, distribution in Ontario never did reach more than about 600,000 quarts a diay. After the introduction of dominion subsidies, in Ontario the distribution of milk reached more than, a million quarts a day, which is ample evidence that the subsidy resulted in bringing up the nutritional standards of the people, particularly of this province. I should say that was the general pattern of the effect in other provinces. I am in favour of the amendment, and would urge the government most strongly to continue the subsidy on milk.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
The moment that this resolution was put before the house I fancy that what went through the minds of the members of the government was, we cannot find money; we cannot afford
Milk Subsidy

this thing. Either the government has meant what it has been saying during the last few years about the new order, or it has not. Here is a right good chance for the government to show whether or not it was deliberately deceiving the people, or whether it really meant what it said.
There is only one way in which the price of goods can be kept from rising, and that is by means of subsidy. At the present time we are in the midst of grave industrial unrest. Everyone knows that one of the major causes of that unrest is a rise in the price of living. Here is another measure proposed by the government which will increase the cost of living. How can we possibly conceive that we shall do away with the industrial unrest in the country when we adopt the very measures which are calculated to bring on industrial unrest?
The government will say, we cannot find the money for a milk subsidy. The government must find the money. The government will say, we cannot tax the people any more. They do not need to tax the people any more. The government will say, we do not want to go into debt any further. They do not need to go into debt any further. I simply say that if the government will take a realistic attitude toward the whole situation of the Canadian economy it will discover how it can keep down the cost of living without increasing taxation and debt. May I warn the government that if it does not adopt a streamlined modem method of dealing with the economic situation in Canada, it is leading the country into disaster, and leading it fast.
I heartily support the amendment made by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). I would say a good deal more if the time were appropriate.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
In supporting the motion I wish to say that the government is ill-advised to take the subsidy off milk, particularly in view of the support which the Canadian people have given to the whole policy of price stabilization. The milk producers of Canada can present facts and figures to prove that even with the fifty-five cent subsidy on a hundred pounds of milk they cannot make money because they are not meeting their cost of production. In fact a demand will be made on the government for an increase in the subsidy. To take it off will place the producers in such a position that milk production will fall off tremendously. The scarcity of milk will increase the price to the consumer. The people in the cities who buy
fMr. Blackmore]
milk will find that the increase of two cents in the price, which in some places will bring it up to fifteen cents a quart, will result in the workers taking the view: What is the use of trying to help the government in maintaining stabilization? What chance is there for us to prevent an increase in the cost of living and the spiral of inflation? The people who have to buy milk for their children, the people who are living on fixed incomes, will find this a terrific hardship, and it will have a detrimental effect upon the economy of Canada and the welfare of the people.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just say a word to urge the government to accept this motion, because the present conditions affecting the production and distribution of milk are of vital importance to the people of Canada. Statements have been made in the press and elsewhere to the effect that if the price of milk goes up, people will not be consuming the quantity of milk they have been consuming during the last five or six years. This will mean that milk production on the farm will be curtailed and less work will be available in rural areas. People who ordinarily work on the farm will flock to the cities, creating a situation such as we had during the depression.
The idea of subsidies is a reasonable one. It is a method of using the taxing power of the country to distribute income, thus increasing production and equalizing the opportunities for consumption. I would urge the government to accept this motion and give consideration to the matter involved.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just one word to say-I am in favour of this motion. As it comes from the opposition, I think it is our duty to demand results from the government. Although our duty may end with demanding results, it is sometimes wise to make suggestions as to how results can be achieved. I am not going to offer any suggestions, because they have been made time and time again from this corner of the house. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has said some mighty things in a few words. If the government cannot do it, if they find that their policy is such that they cannot possibly do it, then the country should know.
I suggest to the government that here is one opportunity of their taking the proposals which have been made over a number of years by the Social Credit group and demonstrating whether or not they are sound. The government do not have to use our proposals to run the economy of the country; all I am suggesting is that in connection with this one

Milk Subsidy
thing, the matter of milk subsidies, they take the proposals we have made over the years. Surely that is not going to upset the whole economy of the country; it is dealing with just one commodity. They should try it, if only as an experiment to see if it will not work. They are challenged to do it; we are demanding results and we suggest that this is the way to do it. I am in favour of the amendment.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my support of this amendment by simply saying this. Surely a government which can vote over $21,000,000 for munitions and arms this year can find a few millions for milk.

maintopic: DISCONTINUANCE OP MILK SUBSIDY-STATEMENT OP MR. KNOWLES-AMENDMENT, MR. NICHOLSON
speechtext:
Tell them about the judges'
salaries.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the feeling of a number of hon. members in regard to this matter, but I am not sure that the mover of the motion (Mr. Nicholson) wishes to do what the motion implies. The acceptance of this motion would prevent the house from going into supply, and I do not think that that is what the hon. member has in mind. I do not think anyone in the house wishes to take that attitude at this moment. I believe what the hon. member wishes to get is an expression of opinion from this house as to the carrying out of a policy which was announced last May. The motion asks that the house record its opinion as to whether consideration should be given to the continuance of the milk subsidy. Whether or not the motion passes, consideration certainly would be given to the continuance of the policy, because consideration is given from day to day to the economy of the nation.
At the present time there are factors in the national economy which were not present last May and which were not present a couple of weeks ago. A serious effort was being made to reconvert from a wartime to a peacetime economy, and it was felt that some day this policy of maintaining prices by government subsidies would have to be abandoned. Last spring it was felt that with respect to the milk subsidy the proper time to do it, in a manner that would1 not be charged as unfair or almost dishonest to the producer was not to cease paying the subsidy at the time milk was most plentiful. It would not have been fair to take off the subsidy at the beginning of a period when the producers were going to have large quantities of milk to which the subsidy would apply. It was thought proper to make an announcement at that time that the consumer subsidy would be removed at once and that the producer subsidy would be removed at the end of the pasture season.
Up to a relatively short time ago the reconversion of the Canadian economy was proceeding in a manner which was looked upon as being fairly satisfactory, but for some reason or other in recent weeks there has been what appears to be a change in the views of a substantial portion of the Canadian people. I refer to certain sections of organized labour. I do not think anyone will dispute the assertion that the only way to maintain our economy on a sound basis is by abundant production. Some sections of organized labour seem to have felt that the way for them to get what they believe they are entitled to is to stop production and hold up the economy of the nation until such time as they can make everybody agree that their share should be such and so. I think that is a most unfortunate development. I think it is a development not only which is harmful to the rest of the Canadian people but which constitutes a shortsighted policy for those sections of organized labour to follow. It has created a difficult position; it has put great pressure upon the price ceilings, and has made it much more difficult to proceed toward a stabilized peacetime economy. These facts are facts which are considered almost every twenty-four hours every day by the government, and would1 be considered whatever was the government in power. Mr. Speaker, the motion before the house is to go into committee of supply. The amendment, which I believe is a proper one, is that consideration be given to the continuance of the milk subsidy, which the government has announced it is withdrawing.
What is the position at the present time? This amendment is in order, or it is not. I suggest respectfully that however much the government may dislike it, it is in order. Being in order it must be dealt with and a vote taken, or withdrawn.
What are the merits of the proposal? In the early days of the war the government came along and said, "We are going to take certain steps to control our economy." Among other things the government said, "We are going to pay a subsidy of two cents on the cost to consumers of their milk, and to producers 55 cents per 100 pounds." When -the first of these proposals was made, the danger we are facing to-day was pointed out by the producers of Canada. The impression it left with Canadian consumers was that they were getting milk for ten cents a quart or thereabouts. As a matter of fact is was costing twelve cents, the extra two cents being paid by the government and charged back to the taxpayers as a whole. But the impression was left with the consumers that they were getting cheap milk.
Now with these subsidies withdrawn there is the impression going around that the cost of milk is going up, that the farmers are thereby deriving some benefit, and the consumers having to pay more. Unfortunately that situation has arisen at the very time when farmers' costs are going up, and when the country finds itself embroiled in strikes and industrial unrest of one kind or another.
This question resolves itself down to this: What is the government's policy? If the government says now that it is going to remove these subsidies. I do not see how hon. members who have moved this amendment can withdraw it. What is the price of con-

Milk Subsidy
tinuing with the amendment, in the event of its being carried? In the first instance we may be delayed for forty-eight hours before we can go into supply again. That of course is only a detail, on a question that merits consideration. With all respect I suggest that the house can get over this impasse and continue its work-if the government is disposed to do it-if the government will undertake to say within the next short period of time whether it intends to persist in withdrawing these subsidies. If it is, there is nothing that can prevent the opposition from taking the stand it is taking in pressing for a vote.
The question is very simple. It is just this. Is the government going to say now, after four or five years of these subsidies, that it is going to make consumers pay the whole cost of the milk, or is it going to continue to take out of the consolidated revenue fund several million dollars to pay two cents on the cost of each quart of milk. I do not remember just what the subsidies to the dairy industry amounted to, but speaking wholly from memory I think they were around $20,000,000. There is not a man in this country but recognizes- that milk production to-day costs more now than it did in the past. And yet these subsidies to the producer and to the consumer are being removed, with the result that the consumer will have to pay more and the producer who needs more will get less.
The government, having a majority in this house and being the government, has the opportunity now of saying whether it will continue its policy or whether it will not. At the moment I am not saying which is right; I am not arguing the merits of the policy at the moment, but I must say that this difficult situation, the government has invited by its policies.
There seems to be a desire to avoid a vote, but I do not see any way of doing it, other than for the government to say: We have heard these representations, and we will consider them and we will let the house know in a short time whether there is to be any change in our policy. speechtext:
I withdraw the
remarks I made about the previous debate, and will proceed now to say what I have to say.
It is an exceedingly dangerous matter for any men charged with responsibility in these dangerous times to lay down hard and specific rules as to what they will or will not do. All that hon. members in the government know is that they face a time of great uncertainty and great danger. Their task is to guide this nation through that great danger, and to come out successfully on the other side.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I consider in view-of what happened this morning that this house is not constitutionally convened. This morning the Acting Prime Minister moved that the house go into committee of supply. An amendment to that motion was moved and carried. That meant that the government was defeated in this house. The government can quote all the rules they like, Beauchesne and any other authorities, but the fact remains that the government made a motion to go into supply this morning and was defeated on the motion. There was only one course open to the government after that defeat. The vote having been taken and the government defeated, before they can go into supply the government must ask the house for a vote of confidence in the government. No such motion was made. According to British parliamentary procedure, when a motion made by any member of the government is defeated in the house the

Supply-Mines and Resources
government is defeated. I realize that certain passages can be quoted from various parliamentary authorities in support of the government; nevertheless the government was defeated this morning on a vote, and as a consequence there was only one thing for them to do and that was to move a vote of confidence in the government. After being sustained on such a vote of confidence it would be the right of the government to move that the house go into committee of supply. That was not done, and I contend that this house is now sitting unconstitutionally, that as the government was defeated on a vote this morning, we are not sitting legally as a parliament.
Ha! Ha!

It is all very well for my hon. friend to say "Ha! Ha!" but there are certain parliamentary rules by which we must abide. I am not so sure but that if a vote of confidence in the government had been moved this morning I might have voted to sustain the government for the time being until the Prime Minister comes home so that we could really give him a defeat. But as it is I contend we are sitting unconstitutionally, and therefore this house should disband right now unless the government is prepared to call the Speaker to the chair and move a vote of confidence in the government.
Did you sit in during the debate this morning?
Yes, and I know more about the rules than you ever did.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
After the vote was taken this morning the Acting Prime Minister moved that the Speaker do now leave the chair. I would refer hon. members to Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, paragraph 489:
When an amendment has been adopted to the motion for the house to go into committee of supply or of ways and means, it may be forthwith moved that the house resolve itself into such committee immediately or on a future day.
That motion was made, that the house go into committee of supply immediately, and the motion .was carried with the unanimous vote of the house. Therefore I must rule that the committee is properly constituted.
There was no vote at all as to whether the house should go into supply immediately. You said, Mr. Chairman, that the house went into committee by unanimous vote of the house. There was no such vote.
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first time that I have heard that the government must resign if it meets an adverse vote in the house. It often happens in every British parliament that a government is defeated on a vote.
Tell me of one case where a government was defeated on a vote.
The British government was defeated on its educational bill at the last session.
And moved a motion of confidence in itself.

I think the usual procedure is that there is an understanding between the government and the opposition as to what will be considered a major vote of want of confidence and what will be considered just an adverse vote on a minor matter. I am quite sure there is nothing in the point, raised by the hon. member for Waterloo South.

I think your decision, Mr. Chairman, is correct. There was a motion moved by the Acting Prime Minister that the Speaker leave the chair, and that was carried unanimously. Therefore I contend that the committee is sitting constitutionally.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, we have often seen questions raised in the house as to the meaning of certain clauses of a bill and heard a minister say: This is what I contend it means. Later the question comes before the courts and a lawyer will say to the court: This is what the minister said' the clause meant. The judge will say: I am1 not concerned with what the minister thought it meant, but with the words of the act itself. I say that under our parliamentary rules the government was defeated this morning, and it should have moved: a vote of confidence in itself, and if that was sustained it should then have moved to go into committee of supply.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: You have given your ruling, Mr. Chairman, that we should proceed with the business of the house. We have lost enough time to-day without losing any more.

Don't try to get away with it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not trying to get away with anything. I am trying to act like a grown-up member of parliament. I do not know whether the hon. member was here or not this morning, but a motion was made and carried that the house go into committee of supply. It is now in committee of supply,

Supply-Mines and Resources
and the chairman has ruled the hon. member's point of order out of order. There has been no appeal from his decision, and I suggest that we now carry on the business of parliament.

Just a minute. I am not going to accept any such speech as that from the Acting Prime Minister. He says he is acting like a grown-up man. If he was a grown-up man he would not have done many things that he has done. He would not have refused the hon. member for Lake Centre many of the documents for which he has asked. He would not have refused to enforce the order in council at Hamilton. So do not let him stand up and say that he talks like a grown-up and that we are children. We were grown-up long before he was there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have heard the further representations that have been made, and I am satisfied that my ruling is correct-
I am not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -and that the committee has been properly constituted and can now proceed with its work.
May I ask the Minister of Justice a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not want to prolong the debate. I will allow one question.

In view of what has taken place here, if that was not a vote of confidence why did the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, speaking on behalf of the government, call for a free vote?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not know that I am required to answer the hon. gentleman. I do not appear to have it here, but my attention was called to a precedent which I have been trying to turn up and which I have not yet put my hand upon, according to which it was determined years ago, in the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that on a motion of tha't kind the government could, if it chose, make it a motion of confidence, but it could also if it chose allow a free expression of the opinions of hon. members on the matter concerned; and that was what was done this morning. There was a declaration by the Minister of Reconstruction that the government was not asking for support on party lines but was asking for an expression of the views of hon. members, and a vote was registered along those lines. Now I think the incident is closed. It was made a condition before the Minister of Reconstruction made that statement that there would be no objection from hon. members to a subsequent motion immediately to go in supply, and it was on the basis of that understanding that the vote was taken, that the

vote was registered, and the motion was made. Those who were present acquiesced in the understanding that had been arrived at; the house went into committee of supply and proceeded with its business, and I think it should continue to do so now.

It is not in my province, of course, to decide whether motions are motions of -want of confidence or not, but for the benefit of the committee may I read from Beauchesne, third edition, paragraph 475:
"Of course there are motions which by themselves carry censure, and such motions would necessarily imply want of confidence in the administration. But when the motion presented is such as this motion, affirming a general principle, not particularly calling question any practice or action of the government, it does not carry with it want of confidence, unless, indeed, it is made so by the will of the administration. If the administration cares to do so, it always has the power to declare that a motion moved in amendment to go into committee of supply is a motion of want of confidence; they have the power, and it follows they can take that course."

speechtext: The hon. member for Regina City asked that he might be allowed, because he has to go away, to discuss the question of the trans-Canada highway, and although it does not properly come within this vote, but rather under item 170, I suggest that the hon. gentleman should have that opportunity.

It has been, but I promised to give the hon. member this opportunity fo discuss it.

I wish to thank the Minister of Mines and Resources for having accorded me the privilege of speaking for a moment or two on this very important subject of the trans-Canada highway, under his departmental estimates. It has been the wish of various hon. members to secure information through questions placed on the order paper with respect to the present status of the highway which ostensibly links the west of Canada to the east, or would do if there were such a thing as a trans-Canada highway, and no department of government has taken a direct responsibility for such a highway, although, to questions I have asked, the Department of Mines and Resources was good enough to prepare a reply.
A few weeks ago in the course of debate the Minister of Agriculture made the statement in this house that it was possible to drive an automobile from eastern Canada to

Supply-Mines and Resources
western Canada remaining entirely on Canadian soil. With that bald statement of the possibility of moving a vehicle on purely Canadian soil there can be no disagreement. However, I have traversed some of the miles to which the Minister of Agriculture referred, and the road is definitely not one which we would call a first-class highway.
I want to place on the record at this time certain information which deals with the general subject of discussion, in the form of replies by the Department of Mines and Resources to questions I asked on July 29, 1946, with regard to the trans-Canada highway. The first question I wish to place on the record is this one:
What mileage of trans-Canada highway is now completed and hard-surfaced (a) in Canada,
(b)	in each of the provinces?
The answer to that question as given by the department was:
No definite standard or specification has been agreed upon or set for a trans-Canada highway, nor has the route of a trans-Canada highway been finally designated. There is a passable road east and west across Canada but it is in various stages- of completion as regards grading, gravelling and paving. While a considerable mileage is hard-surfaced much of it is below modern standards and will have to be rebuilt. The following information is the best available and is based on information recently supplied by the provinces.

It seems to me as a citizen of Canada preposterous that we now call ourselves a middle-class nation when we have as yet no trans-Canada system, or even a recognized route on which the trans-Canada highway system may be some day built. Part of the difficulty, I assume, arises from our unwieldy constitution, if I may use that term, under which the provincial governments have within their prerogative the right to build highways where they please, but the practice has from time to time developed that certain roads are subsidized out of federal government contributions to the provincial governments generally on a fifty-fifty basis. With the growth of the country, it is preposterous that in order to get highway traffic between the eastern section and the west it is necessary for us to go through the Untied States, their national government having seen fit to provide out of the national revenue the funds necessary to make first-class roads.
Various political parties have in the past promised before elections that they would obligate themselves to the construction of a trans-Canada highway system. I do not intend to go over past election promises, but I think it is the almost unanimous wish of the citizens of Canada that we have good highways in these modern times and that the federal government should now take the lead in this very important matter.
I wish to put on the record a resolution which has been forwarded to the dominion government from my own constituency and which sums up the attitude in that part of the country. It is from the Saskatchewan tourist convention held in Regina on May 21 last:
Supply-Mines and Resources

This conference resolves that, regardless of the ultimate outcome of the dominion-provincial conference, an agreement be immediately arranged between Saskatchewan and the federal government for the construction of at least two east-west and at least one north-south hardsurfaced highways in Saskatchewan on the basis of federal responsibility similar to that followed in the United States federal highway system; and further be it resolved that the above programme be commenced this year and completed as speedily as physically possible, not deferring until such time as works of this character are considered necessary as an unemployment measure.
In the course of the discussion this afternoon I am sure reference will be made to the tourist business of Canada. Tourist agencies are set up all across the country for the purpose of attracting visitors to the playgrounds of Canada, which are internationally famous. But unless you fly-and then you must be prepared to take planes equipped with pontoons instead of wheels, so that you land on a lake instead of in a field-you cannot get to the various park centres of the country. The tourist business is recognized as an immensely lucrative one, and it will thrive better, in my opinion, if we make it possible for tourists to bring their families by the means considered modern, namely, the automobile. For tourist reasons as well as for the linking up of east and west in Canada, I suggest that when we prate of Canadian unity we should afford some opportunity for its realization physically through the intermingling of the people. We could reasonably ask the Minister of Mines and Resources to see that his department, or to suggest that some other department, take immediate steps towards implementing a programme for a trans-Canada highway system.

We had that vote before for the building of a hydrogenation plant, but after the war various opinions were obtained with regard to the processes then in vogue, and generally the picture became extremely confused. There was doubt in the mind of the department whether a hydrogenation plant would serve the purpose. We dealt with the matter by appointing a committee headed by Doctor Wallace of Queen's university, Kingston; Doctor Hopkins, vice-president of the Imperial Oil, and J. R. It had evidence before it from experts who knew what the effect of a hydrogenation plant might be. They made a report to me which I hold in my hand, and which may be of interest to the committee. Pilot Hydrogenation Plant Committee Terms of Reference
1.	To review the petroleum resources of Canada. the United States and other countries with reference to future supplies for Canadian consumption. especially in the area of the prairie provinces;
2'. To review methods and progress in producing synthetic liquid fuels in Germany, Great Britain, the United States and other countries with especial reference to actions of governments to produce or stimulate production of these fuels by research or otherwise, and the reasons for such actions;
3.	To obtain information on the nature and extent of raw materials available in Canada for synthetic liquid fuel production and consider
whether hydrogenation as presently known is a fully developed and practical process that can be applied to Canadian raw materials without further research and pilot plant tests;
4.	To consider whether the production of synthetic liquid fuels in Canada is likely to be of future importance in the dominion's economy or for defence purposes and whether there is need for the dominion government to make the capital and operating expenditures necessary to carry on research and operation of a pilot hydrogenation plant to stimulate production;
5.	To report to the dominion government what action, if any, the committee considers the government should take with respect to research on hydrogenation and erection of a pilot hydrogenation plant, taking into account the following questions:
(a)	Whether a long period would elapse before it would become necessary to produce synthetic liquid fuels from Canadian coal;
(b)	Whether Canadian oil companies can be expected without government research to undertake utilization of heavy refinery residues for production of lighter petroleum products;
(c)	Whether the dominion government should stimulate production of motor fuels from Alberta bitumen by carrying on research into hydrogenation and by operation of a pilot hydrogenation plant;
(d)	Whether the processes and economies of hydrogenation have been sufficiently determined to be applicable to Canadian raw materials, such as coal, crude petroleum, refinery residues and Alberta bitumen, without it being necessary for the dominion government to assist industry by pilot plant operation;
(e)	Whether hydrogenation research is warranted and not too far removed from present-day Canadian problems to warrant dominion government expenditure.
Report of the Committee Appointed to Advise
on the Proposal to Construct a Hydrogenation Pilot Plant by the Department of Mines and Resources
The committee, having heard and considered the facts and data which were submitted and which accompany this report, are reporting as follows:
Firstly-referring directly to the terms of reference, the committee have the following comments:
1.	There is no world shortage of petroleum nor in supply of crude petroleum from the gulf coast regions of the United States or from South America. There is, however, a possible future shortage from the mid-continental regions of the United States, and conservation policies may limit future exports from the United States.
The crude oil required by eastern Canada and British Columbia, constitutes some 80-85 per cent of the total Canadian requirements, has been imported from the United States and South America. From the data given a larger proportion of the future imports for eastern ( anada may come from South America or other countries than the United States, but no shortage of supply is envisaged for some considerable time.
The prairie provinces' requirements are at present largely supplied from Alberta production which is, however, declining. Consequently new sources of crude oil for the prairie provinces are required.
2.	Production of synthetic liquid fuels from coal has been developed further in Germany than in any other country, in large measure due to a policy of national self-sufficiency. Great Britain has also established synthetic
Supply-Mines and Geology

liquid fuel production from coal. Both Germany and Great Britain used high pressure hydrofenation technique, although in Germany the iseher-Tropsch technique was also being used. On the data presented, cost of synthetic liquid fuels from coal in Great Britain and Germany exceeded cost of imported petroleum.
No commercial synthetic liquid fuel plants have been established in the United States, although both government and industry are undertaking large scale research in this field. United States research programmes into synthetic liquid fuels from coal are based on long-range planning rather than on immediate use, and both hydrogenation and the improved Fischer-Tropsch technique are being studied.
Processes for the production of synthetic liquid fuels from natural gas have been developed by industry in the United States, making use of the fluid catalyst technique and an improved Fischer-Tropsch catalyst, to a point where manufacture is claimed to be commercially feasible with low cost natural gas.
3.	The raw materials available in Canada are natural gas, natural bitumen from the oil sands of Alberta and coal. Plentiful supplies of coal suitable for hydrogenation are available in the prairie provinces and there are substantial coal reserves in the maritime provinces which are also suitable. The oil sands of Alberta are a large potential supply of bitumen. The natural gas reserves of Alberta and of western Saskatchewan are large and recent developments suggest that they may be sufficiently large to prove an important source of raw material for synthetic liquid fuel for the prairie provinces.
High pressure hydrogenation, as developed in Europe, is not directly applicable to natural gas. A high pressure hydrogenation plant, based on European technique, could probably be designed in Europe for treatment of either bitumen or Canadian coals, although, in either case, large scale tests in Europe would first be desirable. Alternatively, pilot plant tests are required in Canada or the United States.
An improved Fischer-Tropsch process for treatment of natural gas as already stated, has been developed in the United States and pilot plant operations have been established. It can be considered a feasible commercial operation.
4.	Production of synthetic liquid fuel in the prairie provinces at reasonable cost will be of importance to the prairie economy and, consequently, to Canadian economy within a comparatively short period unless new oil fields are discovered in the prairie provinces or in the adjoining states to the south.
Synthetic liquid fuel production in eastern Canada and on the Pacific coast appears unlikely to be of importance for some time to come.	.
5.	On the basis of the evidence and data submitted while the committee feel that further research and experimental pilot plant work should proceed in the field of synthetic liquid fuels, they also feel that further study must be undertaken before final plans can be developed which will ensure best results from the proposed expenditure.
Secondly-In addition to answering the terms of reference 1-5 specifically, the summary and conclusions of your committee are as follows: il. Synthetic liquid fuel research would primarily apply to the needs of the prairie provinces.
2.	The supply of crude petroleum products from the prairie provinces will in all probability prove inadequate for the prairie needs, as the reserves in known domestic fields will not meet the increasing demand.

3.	Sources of raw material for synthetii liquid, fuels in the prairie provinces are natural gas, bitumen from the Alberta oil sands and coal. In any research project which may be undertaken, the relative availability and value of these three resources of raw materials must be continuously kept in mind. Further study is needed on this comprehensive level.
4.	The synthesis of gas to liquid fuels is being actively investigated at the present time in connection with commercial installations. Costs are lower than for either coal or petroleum. Assuming adequate supplies, natural gas would appear to be the most suitable source of synthetic liquid fuels for the prairie provinces.
5.	Recent work in the United States applying to fluid catalyst technique is of such importance that it must receive further study and consideration before any final decision can be reached as to the type of pilot plant which might be installed for experimental work on bitumen or coal.
6.	The United States is planning large scale research on synthetic liquid fuels from coal by both direct hydrogenation and by Fischer-Tropsch technique. If close cooperation is maintained with this work, research in Canada might very properly be directed to the utilization of bitumen from the Alberta oil sands.
7.	Inasmuch as the evidence submitted indicates that cost of separating the bitumen from the oil sand is at present too high for economic utilization and inasmuch as separation and processing must be dealt with together, further research of the relative value of bitumen as compared with coal as a raw material should be undertaken before a major programme is instituted.
8.	The considerations in favour of establishing an experimental pilot plant in the west near the source of raw material and where future commercial operations might be undertaken should be again carefully reviewed before a decision as to location is finally reached. Integration of the pilot plant operations with the existing government synthetic gas ammonia plant at Calgary should also receive the most careful consideration.
9.	It is the opinion of your committee that further study must be given to the problem of synthetic liquid fuel research as a whole before final plans are initiated: and that it will take at least six months to obtain the necessary information dealing with raw materials. processes and United States research programmes. In this connection your committee would point out that, even by making use of existing plans, it would probably take about two years to complete designs, let contracts and erect a large scale pilot plant. In the further studies that are. in your committee's opinion, required, the cooperation of industry should be secured in order that duplication of effort may be avoided and the most suitable research plan and pilot plant may be developed.
10.	Having in mind the basic importance to Canadians of fuel problems in general and the fact that research work in the field of synthetic liquid fuels is closely related to and common to other fuel problems, your committee recommend the establishment of a fuel research board representative of the Department of Mines and Resources, the national research council, the research council of Alberta, and private industry, which should direct an overall programme of fuel research. Synthetic liquid fuel is one of the more urgent problems to be dealt with.
11.	The members of the committee wish to reoord their warm appreciation of the able presentations by officers of the department and by officials from the United States and from

It is the intention of the department to implement that recommendation and to make the appointment of a fuel research board for this purpose. In view of the further study that the committee considered should precede the development of plans for a synthetic liquid fuel pilot plant, the laboratory building item previously in the estimates of the Department of Public Works has been dropped for the present. Of the vote of $770,000 which stood in the mines and geology branch estimates for equipping of the plant, a revote of only $50,000 is required in order to maintain and preserve what is already in the hands of the department. This will be used for remodelling the present small scale equipment so that it can be employed for experimental work. I can tell the hon. gentleman that we are very seriously concerned. I did not want to spend $770,000 when it was not confirmed that we would receive any value from it afterwards. In the light of the evidence which was given before the committee and the recommendations they made, we thought we would defer the spending of money until we were sure that we would get the results from it. As I say, we intend to confirm that with the fuel research board and pursue the matter further and develop it the best we can in the light of actual circumstances which we now know since the war.
I notice that it is a hydrogenation plant.
Yes.
Has the department given any consideration to the method of processing fuel known as low temperature carbonization?
Yes; I am informed that studies of that have been made.
The department is not concentrating completely on the hydrogenation process?

It will be found from the discussion before the committee to which I referred that all phases of fuel problems were discussed. We are not directing our activities solely to the one process of hydrogenation. We shall get the best we can before spending money, in order that we shall have something worth while in the end.

Personally I am in favour of the low temperature process. I am not going to go into that at any length at the moment,
but I believe Canadian fuels are adaptable to the low temperature carbonization process. It is workable. One can get a practical demonstration of it in Burlington, Ontario. A man by the name of Caunt has a pilot plant there. He has been in Ottawa for many years trying to sell the idea. Personally I am sold on it, I have read considerably on it. Germany had a method of processing fuels, and it is used to a great extent in the old country. If we are to be successful in fuel research, low temperature carbonization is the method which should be applied to Canadian fuels. When the board is set up I hope the minister will see to it that due consideration is given to the low temperature process.
Yes.

Doctor Warren of the department was sent to Germany and he made a study of these matters and brought it before the committee of which I have already spoken. It was one of the subjects of discussion. In the light of that discussion and of other evidence that was given, we thought it best that research should be made not only in connection with that process but in connection with all forms of synthetic fuel processes.

To give some idea of their aims I shall read part of a letter which they have been sending out.
In the year 1876 the Battleford mounted police post was established by Colonel James Walker and linked up with such posts as MacLeod, Ft. Walsh, Calgary, Edmonton, Carlton and Swan river. This force served the north-west council 1878-1881 at Battleford. It served the Department of Indian Affairs. From this point its force went forth to battle at Duck lake. Carlton, Cutknife, Fort Pitt and Frenchman's Butte. Later, during the settlement days, it became a stabilizing and encouraging factor in our civilization. This locality is the home of the Cree Indian. In the early days it successfully held back the Blackfoot. There are also tribes at Saulteaux, Assiniboine and Sioux, with their long history and cultural development. The Indian agency office is still located here. The little red brick building which, served as an office is still standing on the north west council hill. Such early explorers as MeGilli-

vray Pink, Cocking, Frobisher, Pond, Henry, Pangman, Umfreville, Thompson and Harmon passed up the North Saskatchewan and crossed to the Beaver river and Isle a la Crosse to Churchill. Their fur post sites are still to be seen. It has been a pleasure to search for these and have professor A. S. Morton come up from Saskatoon and cheek them over. These posts should be rebuilt or remarked, and {lie thrilling story of early fur days retold: Manchester House, Pine Island Post, Eagle Hills Post, Turtle Post, Buckingham House. Ihe rich fur and pemmican trade of the Hudson's Bay and North-West Company was centred in this part of the Saskatchewan river and at Green lake, Isle 5 la Crosse, Prince Albert and Edmonton. As our young citizens grew up in the midst of this rich romantic and sacrificial story tliev too caught the spirit of enterprise. Such localities gave their best youth to the first and second world wars when the call came.
Peace has come again to our beloved Canada. A new youth is re-examining our national life. It asks, "How can harmony, brotherhood and culture be advanced and what shall we save in a new civilization?" Shall we study the social and economic factors of our localities in such a way to engender love for nobler purposes and make the land blossom and sing? It is a land with a tradition and a promise. What shall be done with these historic spots? Once more we have asked the government to help. The Saskatchewan government consented to renovate the famous mounted police barracks. This cluster of some dozen buildings has been standing idle since 1923. The superintendent's house, tlie inspector's house, the gaol, the hospital. stable and mess room are to be saved.
It was originally intended to take down the mess room. But they have been receiving so many relics and so many things they would like to save that it 'has now been decided to try to save this building so that it may be used as a museum. My purpose in rising this afternoon is to ask the government to make a small grant toward having a museum in that building. The letter continues:
The renovation work commenced in August 1945. Two of the main buildings are ready for use. Our citizens suggested a mounted police memorial and Indian museum. The government accepted this plan provided citizens would furnish and equip this memorial and museum. The challenge was accepted. I could go on to tell more about the project, but I do not wish to take up too much time. I hope that the government will take an interest in this museum, because as I said at the outset, it is unique; there is nothing to match it in Canada. It would be a shame if these old historic forts were allowed to go to rack and ruin and finally disappear. If we can save them and make use of them in a cultural and educational way I am sure it will be worth while. If the minister will see that

there is something placed in the estimates, only one or two thousand dollars to help finish the project, it will be deeply appreciated by the people in that district.
The hon. member has already spoken to me about this. I shall place this matter before the historic sites committee, because it would come under their control.

I would ask the minister and his officials to consider whether the time has not arrived when we should have a large national museum here in Ottawa. Many precious materials found throughout the country, which can be traced to pioneer days, are now being lost. Large quantities of new materials, on the other hand, are being discovered. A national museum in Ottawa would house those priceless relics. Only to-day I was talking to a former employee' of the government about communications instruments. They comprise only one group. There are multitudes of other types of materials; and we should have all these early Canadian relics of one kind or another displayed in the national capital.
As we get along further I should like to see a building of that kind, and plans could be organized now. One such building is to be seen in Washington. There they have a national museum to display the vast relic treasures of their country. In Canada much of this is being lost because of the lack of an appropriate place in which to put it.

51/0. Maintenance of plant of Abasand Oils Limited, $50,000.	.
Is the minister going to make a statement on this item?

The hon. gentleman has spoken to me about this project, in which he has been very much interested for many years. The hon. member for Athabaska is also much in-

Supply-Mines and Geology
terested. I reviewed the project last year. The government undertook as a war emergency project to finance rehabilitation of the plant of Abasand Oils Limited, near Fort McMurray, Alberta, and to carry out pilot plant operations on the mining and treatment of bituminous sands. Test runs of the renovated separation plant commenced in June, 1944, and a considerable amount of information was gained regarding the process which the Abasand Company had used prior to the agreement with the government, namely, the McClave hot-water process of separating bitumen from the sands. Early in 1945 a new method of recovering the bitumen was being developed and appeared to have definite advantages, as separation was performed at room temperature with a very considerable economy in heat consumption. Equipment installed for this new process was about to be brought into operation when the separation plant, workshops and warehouse were destroyed by fire on June 16, 1945.
In my review of the project I pointed out that although the cost data obtained could not be regarded as conclusive the approximate estimates indicated that commercial utilization of the sands depended not only on securing much lower costs of mining and treating the sands, but upon processing the extracted bitumen so as to produce a large proportion of the high-priced petroleum products. A large scale refinery, of the order of 10,000' barrels a day capacity and employing either a catalytic cracking or hydrogenation process, was seen as necessary for low cost operation.
The government entered upon the project under the stress of a wartime emergency requiring every effort to be put forward to obtain oil supplies. Abasand Oils Limited transfererd its properties, mining rights and process rights to the government for the sum of SI under the agreement, which is to terminate 180 days after the date of proclamation by the government that the state of war has ceased. The deferred settlement provisions of the agreement give the government the right to pay Abasand Oils Limited for its properties, mining rights and processes as existing when the agreement was entered into. If the government does not wish to exercise its option the company has the right to reassume the titles to its properties and mining rights and processes, and to assume ownership of the government's investment in plant, by making suitable settlement with the government for its expenditure. If neither party desires to exercise its option, the agreement contains provision 63260-343J
for disposing of the plant and rights and for apportionment of the proceeds as the respective interests may appear.
The government did not purchase the ownership or stock of Abasand Oils Limited. Under the agreement the company placed its-titles in the hands of the government and it entered into the position of being an agent, or contractor in expending government moneys, through its board of directors, on improving the plant and operating it to develop tar sands-treatment processes. The company is still a private corporation fully entitled, if the government does not wish to pay for its assets, to recover its business.
Good reason would not seem to exist for the dominion government remaining in an oil enterprise in peace time. The government, therefore, has not proceeded with financing the rebuilding of the separation plant destroyed in the fire, although the board of directors have desired to rebuild and install the new separation process for operations at an approximate capacity of 600 tons of sand per day. The proposal submitted by the board was that the government should provide $700,000 for rebuilding and operation of the plant for one year and that moneys recovered from fire insurance should be applied towards this proposed expenditure. The board maintained that it was necessary to have operations extend over a period of one year in all types of weather in order to demonstrate that a successful separation process has been achieved and that without such a demonstration by the pilot plant the investment by private enterprise of many millions of dollars for establishment of a large-scale refinery could not be expected. The board also expressed the view that abandonment of the project by the government would not only delay development of the tar sands resource but would destroy any hope of salvaging the investment not only of the government but of private enterprise. Abasand Oils has stated that its investment in plant and rights, before the government entered into the agreement, amounted to well over a million dollars.
The position of the Abasand project is that out of allotments of $2,300,000 from war appropriation and war and demobilization appropriations in the fiscal years 1943-44, 1944-45 and 1945-46, expenditures of $1,949,077.52 had been made to March 31, 1946, and revenues of $28,784.99 had been received and deposited in the consolidated revenue fund. The net expenditure to the end of the last fiscal year was, therefore, $1,920,292.53. Since the end of the fiscal year there has been
