received and deposited in the consolidated revenue fund proceeds of insurance amounting to $374,676.55. After credit of the insurance proceeds the net outlay of government on this project to March 31, 1946, has been *1,545,615.98. By means of this expenditure the government has assisted the company in developing mining methods and in the development of a partly-proven new separation process, and has a substantial investment in a rebuilt refinery, power plant, and office and townsite buildings.
With the close of hostilities the wartime emergency in which the Abasand. project had its inception came to an end. Consequently, negotiations are now being carried on with the Abasand board of directors for the return of the company's mining rights and titles on a basis which would give the government a reasonable and equitable eventual settlement for its investment if future operations should prove successful. In these negotiations full cognizance must be taken of the company's contractual rights under the agreement and of its right to a part of the insurance proceeds representing original company property destroyed in the fire.
Pending the conclusion of an equitable arrangement with Abasand Oils Limited the government continues to hold the titles and to be responsible for the properties and rights. Because of the obligation incumbent upon the government until the titles and rights are returned it has been necessary that the estimates contain a provision of $50,000 for maintenance of the plant.
Subsequent to that, drilling took place in the Abasand fields which showed that there was liquid bitumen there which gave hopes that there might be some degree of success in operating these sands, and a request was made of the department that we should not now discontinue drilling operations because there were favourable prospects in several of the holes which had been drilled. If we had stopped operations then and subsequently had attempted to drill the sands again, our staff and equipment by that time might have disappeared. The company therefore proposed and we accepted that, rather than drop the project, we would explore the possibilities of liquid bitumen in these fields, which if it was in sufficient quantities might be a good commercial prospect. Accordingly, in the next item, 541, I am asking for a sum of money for drilling in these sands. If that is successful, and the company seems to be hopeful that it will be, I may say bluntly that we expect that this will be the last operation the government will undertake in these fields.
We are drilling now. Some reports though not all, have been received. There is, if not a considerable hope, certainly a degree of hope that they may find there liquid bitumen which, if in sufficient quantities, would probably make this a prosperous commercial field. When that $100,000 which has been asked for is expended the results will be given to the company, and they are hopeful that they can carry on and expend their own money with advantage. They spent about a million dollars on the project before the government entered into it, and they are willing to take the chance of going ahead and operating as a company, and the government will then step out of the picture. I thought the committee ought to be informed of this. The company has been the subject of a good deal of comment and many optimistic opinions have been expressed. I am sure that what has been done by the government in exploring this area will be of benefit; and we feel that, having done this, they can take over. In the meantime we will transfer the titles of the properties to them, and pay to them a portion of the insurance money which we now hold and to which they may be entitled, the money to be paid over when the settlements are being made.

Owing to the lateness of the session I shall speak very briefly. I should like to go into the whole story, but not now. When the estimates of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply were before the house I promised to go into the matter, but it is now too late.
The whole business connected with the government operation of the Abasand is a tragedy of the first water. I am happy to hear that the government is going to get out of it, apart from continuing to drill the sands to ascertain if there is oil or rich bitumen there-. With that decision I am in hearty agreement; it is related to vote 141. The minister knows that I have been up to that plant on several different occasions. He has said that definite results have been obtained. As far as I know from those on the job there are no worthwhile results; no definite results have been obtained; and this is borne out by one of the minister's last statements in reference to the new plant which was burned down before definite results were obtained after it was brought into operation. That is true. The establishment was burnt down almost on the day it commenced operation. That was the third plant erected up there. It is an evidence of the impossibility of trying to operate any commercial enterprise from three or four thousand miles away^that is, from Ottawa. I am not finding fault with anyone in Ottawa who had to do wdth it.

Those here did their best, but they could not be up there and in Ottawa at the same time. I for one am very glad to know that the government is getting out of it and will give a private company a chance to take it over and, if they wish to do so, build a new plant; that is what is required.
As the minister has said, the country itself has already put up a net amount of $1,545,000, after deduction of insurance from the gross amount, and that is enough for us to put into it, outside of the drilling of the sands. My recommendation would be, since the government have all the equipment up there and have contractors on the job, that they continue to drill over the area which is now being drilled over to prove the richness of the deposits, near Steep Bank river. The Alberta government took over the former Fitzgerald plant, about forty miles down the river from Fort McMurray. There they have obtained very good results. I am thoroughly conversant with his process, and, contrary to what the minister read, the McClave process is a good one. I have that from men who have been in the tar sand business for many years. But no one can tell the worth of the process on which the government has spent so much money. I am not going into that matter because it is past and gone. As I have said, I am so pleased to hear the minister say that the government are getting out of it, but that they are going to continue drilling down the Athabaska river near Steep Bank river, which is a small river that flows in on the right bank of the Athabaska river, that I shall refrain from pursuing any further this Abasand business at present and am prepared as far as I am concerned to let these items go through.

What is the purpose of these investigations in mineral economics, and what has been achieved by them in the past? Why is it considered worth while to spend money on them? It is not easy for an ordinary member to get a comprehension of what is involved.

I might give a brief explanation of the vote. The chaotic conditions in which the world finds itself at the close of world war II necessitate continuous investigation of the economic effect these conditions are likely to have on Canada's, mining, metallurgical and allied chemical industries.
In the immediate post-war period and for some time afterward, many problems will confront these industries; those that will be paramount will be economic, not technological. Consequently many studies must be made in anticipation of problems that bear upon home and foreign markets for Canadian products, Canada's mineral position relative

to that of other countries, Canada's mineral reserves and mineral deficiencies, operating costs, cartels, competitive products, subsidies, new uses for minerals and mineral products, et cetera. More valuable assistance could, too, with this increase in activities. be given to the departments of Finance and National Revenue in problems of the character concerning which they ordinarily solicit the help of the mines and geology branch.
Because the existing staff of the division of economics could satisfactorily handle only a relatively small percentage of the problems enumerated above, the cabinet committee on reconstruction, on the recommendation of the Minister of Reconstruction, approved on May 18, 1945, a commencement of this work, and on July 23, 1945, treasury board approved a temporary establishment of eight positions. In connection with fees and berths, I took the matter up last year- perhaps the minister will remember it-as it applied to Riding Mountain national park, in which we have a common interest since it is situated in the minister's constituency and right next to mine. At that time I drew attention to the timber berth owned by the Northern Trust Company, and attempted to find out more about it, but we were not able to come to much of a conclusion. Since that time I have been asking for a number of returns, as the minister may know, and I have gathered some information. There are a number of things which I should like to understand at this time. First of all in my opinion the fees which have been charged have not been very provident from the point of view of the treasury. The fees for lumber have been $1 a thousand. I realize that the company has been holding this limit for a long time. It is no longer the policy, of the government to sell berths in that way. From
the returns I have received I have worked out a simple calculation which shows that since 1889, which appears to be the first date on which this timber limit was held, the company has taken out 13,562,000 feet of lumber, exclusive of other timber products. According to the regulations they pay 81 a thousand which would amount to $13,562-I am leaving the other things aside for a moment, because the fees differ. In another return which I asked for last year it was indicated that a Mr. DeWitt of Sandy Lake took a permit in 1941-42 for 1,253,482 feet of lumber for which he paid $4.75 a thousand. I realize that there is some difference between a permit holder and a licensee in the other fees they have to pay, royalties and so on. But in the matter of lumber alone the difference of price between $1 and $4.75 is substantial. I have worked out some rough figures which show that had the trust company had to pay the same amount as this private individual had to pay in 1941-42, over that period of time they would have paid $64,419 instead of $13,562, which leaves a potential loss to the government of over $50,000. Some of that will be recovered in ground rents, royalties, and so on, but the net loss will still be a great deal of money. I cannot see the justification for allowing these timber limits to continue, with the price of lumber what it is to-day, regardless of what the policy used to be.
Here is a company which evidently has something of a monopoly in that park, and which is able to get its lumber at $1 a thousand, while other people who come in and1 bid for lumber, if they are successful in getting a permit, will have to pay up to $4.75 to get the same kind of lumber. While I am on this subject I should like to say that I took a little time to investigate this limit. I think my figures are correct, because I received them from the foreman of the saw mill. I believe the minister is familiar with the mill about which I am speaking. In December of last year the price of rough lumber at the mill ranged from $41 to $49 wholesale. That was the price if you took it away; if it was delivered there would be an additional charge. This is the same lumber which they were obtaining for $1 a thousand.
In addition I found that farmers who obtained a permit to cut logs in that limit were obliged to bring their logs to that saw mill, since it was the only one operating in there- as I say, it was a monopoly-and they were practically forced-because there was no other arrangement that I could learn about-to accept half the lumber cut from the logs which they brought to the mil'. In other words, if

logs were cut which would yield 2,000 feet of lumber, you would get only 1,000; the saw mill would get the other 1,000 as their part of the bargain. When lumber was selling at the mill at as high as $49 a thousand, that was a substantial amount to take from the farmer in return for the sawing of his product.
I also found that the farmer did not have much choice in the quality of lumber which he got, because at the time he brought his logs in to the saw mill there was no good lumber to take. There was no sawing going on at the time. They just piled up his logs, and he had the choice of either getting his lumber from the pile or waiting or coming back at the time of the sawing season. When I look at regulations like this I wonder whether we really have free enterprise. I see no reason, why a person, simply because he may have been of the right political shade some years ago, should be given a favourable contract of this kind so that to-day he is able to get these things at these favourable rates. There is no possibility of a man with a small sawmill being able to compete, if we -want to put it that way, with someone who is in a monopolistic and favourable position. I cannot see any justification for this and, if the minister can explain it, I shall be glad to hear his explanation.

Provided that such renewal shall be subject to the payment of such rental and dues and to such terms and conditions as are fixed by the regulations in force at the time renewal is made.
If we go through the rest of the regulations we find that the minister has the power to make regulations, which I think is proof that the minister may set the fees from year to year according to what he thinks is proper. I think that has been the case in connection with timber limits or permits on Indian reserves. In those cases the fees are substantially higher than those charged licensees under these regulations. I believe it is quite definite, that the minister has the right to set the fees from year to year.
The only argument which I think the minister can use is that a contract was entered into at the time the timber berth was sold some years ago and that he is not disposed now to change the terms of that contract. I do not think that is a good argument, because times have changed. The prices that prevailed when this company took over the timber berths in 1889 and 1898 are different from the prices that prevail to-day. Retail prices of lumber, shingles, lath and all these things have gone up tremendously, and there is no reason why the minister should not change the regulations to bring these prices up to compare with the present scale of prices.
I believe the treasury of the country is losing a substantial amount of money each year because, of the favourable contracts held by these companies. I do not want to go into the matter of Indian reserves at the present time because it comes under a different vote. But I would point out that over the last five years 100 million feet of lumber have been taken out of the Indian reserves alone. I have here several returns showing the number of feet of lumber and other products taken from dominion crown lands. A simple calculation shows that we are losing thousands of dollars, perhaps hundreds of thousands of dollars each year because the scale of fees is still in many cases what it was at the time the companies were formed, or at the time the 63260-344
individuals got their timber berths; and they are not comparable with prices people now pay for lumber and other timber products.

The question has been asked as to why the timber dues were not raised to the same level as those charged by the province outside the park and by the dominion for timber permits under the park regulations.
In regard to the rates charged on timber berths, I would point out that these berths were not operated for many years prior to 1936. From 1936 until the war years the operator of these berths was carrying on under depression conditions, at which time he was required to sell his lumber at cheap prices. This was a definite benefit to the community, and it was felt at this time that we could not justify raising the rates. The dues on timber cut under park regulations were raised on November 2, 1940, to what the province was charging outside the park. The chief reason for this increase in dues was to discourage applications for timber permits in the park and to force all those who could secure their timber under more favourable conditions from provincial sources to do so. There is only a limited amount of timber which can be made available each year in the park.
In regard to the operations on the two licensed timber berths, the value of timber has changed greatly during the war years, but any time the wartime prices and trade board were consulted in regard to raising rates we were advised that it was not in accordance with government policy to raise such rates. Such a policy is still in force, and therefore in the meantime there is nothing which can be done in this connection. However, I think that as soon as the wartime restrictions are lifted the department proposes to (a) raise the rates on these licensed berths to what the province is charging; and (b) see that definite steps are taken in accordance with the licence to have the commercial timber cut and the cut-over areas withdrawn each year as the area is cut over.

What is being done under this item? I think we have come to the stage in our development ir Canada, as far as timber is concerned, where something must be done and done quickly; otherwise we shall lose what has been one of the most valuable economic assets this country has had. There is scarcely a province in Canada- that is not almost denuded of forest wealth, which at one time we thought would never be destroyed or be exhausted. How many forest stations are in operation and what work is being done m them?

We are spending very much more now than we did before the war, nearly three times the amount. This vote is for the conduct of research work on five forest experiment stations and outside demonstration areas under the supervision of the stations as follows: Acadia, in New Brunswick, area 35 square miles; Yalcartier, in Quebec, area 7% square miles, which was closed for the duration owing to the superintendent being on military service; Petawawa, in Ontario, area 97 square miles; Riding Mountain, area 2514 square miles, within the Riding Mountain national park, Manitoba; Kananaskis, in Alberta, area 63 square miles.
These stations function as field laboratories for conducting silvicultural research and investigations in stands representative of the various forest regions in which they are located and in accordance with policies and plans evolved by the senior technical staff at headquarters.
With the end of the war and the greatly increased interest evident on the part of provinces, industry and the general public in Canada's forest resources, it becomes necessary to revise and expand the activities of the dominion forest service during the post-war period. Most of the labour during the war years was performed by alternative service workers at nominal rates of pay, and normal work had in the main to be drastically curtailed and reduced to a care and maintenance -basis. It now becomes necessary not only to resume normal programmes, but to expand these on a basis designed to meet the requirements of a new era being ushered in during the post-war years.

This particular restriction has undoubtedly created serious inconvenience in some sections of the country, particularly in those areas affected by a heavy influx of tourists and by the repatriation of men from the forces and their families.

As hon. members already know, we were able to exceed our combined commitments on wheat flour and other cereals for the crop year ended July 31. Last year I spoke on this item and made a request of the minister, and to refresh his memory I should like to say a few words with reference to our national park in Prince Edward Island.
As hon. members know, Prince Edward Island was discovered in 1534 by that great explorer Jacques Cartier, who was so greatly impressed by the beauty of the island that he wrote in his diary these words:
Low and flat and the fairest That may possibly be seen,
And full of beautiful trees and meadows.
Now, after a little more than four hundred years, Jacques Cartier's description can be intensified by the use of all the best adjectives one can find in Webster's dictionary to do justice to the island. We have a national park. It is one of the latest to be created. Established in 1937, it is a great addition to the tourist playgrounds of Canada. It extends along the north shore of Prince Edward Island for some twenty-five miles or more. While not large, it comprises over 4,000 acres.
It begins at Dalvay-Stanhope down by the sea on Tracadie bay and extends to Covehead harbour and then on to Braekley Beach, which is known to a great many even in this house. It follows along the coast to Rustico bay. The greater portion and perhaps the most interesting part of the park extends from Rustico harbour to the lake of Shining Waters at New London bay, and is known as the Rustico Cavendish part of our national park.
I know the minister has visited the park and had a delightful game of golf on the Green Gables golf course there. He also helped to open our national park. I am not going to dwell on the beauties of this park which, with its woodland beauties and fine bathing beaches, attracts hundreds of tourists, but I should like to mention that the finest advertising Prince Edward Island ever had as a beautiful tourist playground came from that wonderful writer, the late Lucy Maud Montgomery MacDonald, who by her writings did more to advertise the excellencies of Prince Edward Island and the beauties of its seacoa9t bordering our national park than all the advertising done by governments so far.

I suggest that what we are trying to do on behalf of the conservation of wild fowl is to a certain extent putting; the cart before the horse. I say that for two' or three reasons. We are trying to cut down the number of days when a man can shoot ducks and the number of ducks which can be taken a year. That is all to the good; I do' not think anyobdy wants to be a hog in the matter of shooting. But we have a great heritage in Canada in our wild fowl population. I should like to read something Which appeared in the magazine Rod and Gun. The writer says:
All these governments are now keenly conscious of Ruskin's dictum, "God has given this earth for our life. It is a great entail. It. belongs as much to those who come after us as to us, and we have no right, by anything we do. or neglect to do, to involve them in unnecessary penalties or to deprive them of the benefits; which are theirs by right."
This is not merely a question of shooting, and killing ducks. The figures which are quoted in this magazine are interesting and, I think, are worth while putting on record for the information of hon. members:
In 1875, it is estimated that we had 400,000,000 waterfowl. By 1900 there were, perhaps, only 200,000,000 and, by 1933, just seven per cent, or 28,000.000 of the 1875 waterfowl! population was left on the continent. In the' short space of 60 years 93 per cent of all waterfowl had disappeared and the balance w'as in a fair way to follow the fate of . . . other species of wild life now extinct.
We should try to find out the cause of this; condition. There are a great many reasons-for the depletion other than destruction by shooting. With the development of the prairies and other parts of our country much: of the water supply dried up. The fowl would bring up their young, and in a short time the water would dry up and the youngsters would die.
As the minister knows, a great work has been done by Ducks Unlimited, but a great deal more remains to be done. We in Canada have a great trust in the matter of our wild fowl population. Most of the ducks nest up in the north country, although certain classes nest in Ontario and other provinces. Ducks Unlimited, consisting of public-spirited men inL

Supply-Lands and Parks
the United States, have spent some millions of dollars on conservation measures. They are aware that the United States cannot do anything directly about the nesting grounds of the ducks which come down and winter in the United States, because the nesting grounds are located in Canada. We, therefore, as Canadians have a duty to do all we possibly can to conserve for future generations the wild fowl of this country. I cannot speak too strongly on this matter. Shooting ducks is a great recreation, and, so far as we members of parliament are concerned, is likely to be the only one open to us this year, since we are not going to have any summer holidays. Let us see if we can do anything to further this enterprise.
Two or three considerations occur to me. We need more money spent in the north country to conserve the water supply, although much is being done in that direction at the present time. I am not much in favour of spending the country's money, but it would be worth our while to 'make a grant to Ducks Unlimited to assist in the work they are carrying on in Canada.
In this connection we have neglected the problem of predatory birds. We see flocks of crows around all the time. We see numbers of starlings outside these buildings. We have horny owls and other predatory birds that are destroying our young broods of ducks, and not only those, but the young partridge, the prairie chicken and other game birds and lovely fowl we have in this country. I think it might be worth while to give a lead to the people and help to preserve, not only for Canada but for the United States, the wild fowl population of this country.

I want to commend the minister for this-limited-grant in the estimates. I was much interested in the eloquent and forceful remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's. We in my part of the country are greatly concerned with the protection of the migratory birds. We have a peculiar condition there which needs special consideration and which I wish to place before the minister. The citizens of the straits of Chignecto, Cumberland county and Westmorland county, in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, are anxious to protect these ducks and geese. They have done a great deal to protect them with their clubs, by having special guardians on the grounds in the closed season, and by planting bird food, wild oats and wild rice. For a great many years they have had a season, which opens on September 15 and which closes earlier, because the birds leave earlier, than in other parts of Nova Scotia
and New Brunswick. I can understand the desire of the minister and the department to have the seasons as uniform as possible; but there is a request, almost a demand, from the people who are interested in the protection of the birds and1 in the sport, that an exception be made in that area and that the earlier season in that part of the two provinces be continued rather than have it open on October the first.
The gunners in the town of Amherst, the town of Sackville, the town of Moncton and in the contiguous country, who have organizations for the protection of birds, met recently and passed resolutions asking that the minister perpetuate the date of the opening of the season, as has been the practice for many years, on September 15. The birds arrive in that district later than in other parts of Nova Scotia and they leave earlier. When they come in the spring they are protected - by the public, but they do a great deal of damage to the newly cropped land, the marsh lands, the hay fields and the newly seeded land by pulling up the roots and destroying crops. The people who are interested in the birds are satisfied to put up with that but they would like the season fixed to suit their conditions. There are some people-a few-who have leased lands or who own large acreage, who are able to get what gunning they desire during a late season. But the men I am speaking about, these members of the gunning clubs composed of industrial workers who work in the factory or on farms, have no other opportunity for an outing. They have been enjoying these outings for many years and they ask that the season be opened on September 15 as heretofore.
I will not ask the minister to make any definite decision now, but I would make a further appeal to him. I have already, together with the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), had conferences with the minister and his officers and have put before them the facts, and I should like the minister to make a statement now giving us an assurance that he will personally give the matter further consideration and see whether he cannot meet the special wishes of these gunners. They do not get nor do they want big bags. It is not for commercial shooting in their case, but for sporting in the widest sense of the term, that they make this request.

I wish to align myself with the hon. member for Cumberland in this matter. Cumberland county and Westmorland lie together at the head of the bay of Fundy. A great many birds are bred in the

Chignecto area. I have been receiving protests from the fish and game protective association branch in Sackville and also in Moncton against the recent order in council changing the date from September 15 to October 1. The men in that locality are not what one might call game hogs. They are prepared to go along with the government in its effort to meet the treaty arrangements with the United States for the preservation of birds, and they are also prepared to go to the extent of cutting down the daily bag and the total bag, but they want an opportunity to shoot. The birds start, to leave in the first or second week in October and . by the middle of October there is practically no shooting. This means that if the season begins on the first of October they get about two weeks. They are willing to cut down on the number of birds they shoot, but they want to have an opportunity to shoot for at least three or four weeks. Most of them have no opportunity at all, except in the evenings. A good many of the men working in the railway shops in Moncton and Sackville foundries and on the farms want to take advantage of that opportunity in the evening to shoot over the decoys, and I urge the minister to give serious consideration to restoring the date to September 15, where it has been for years. There are three zones in New Brunswick. Westmorland is in the large zone, and I have reason to know that the majority of the people in New Brunswick, particularly in the area of that large zone No. 3, want the season to open on September 15. There is a disadvantage, of course, in having it open early because, as. duck hunters know, the early birds have too many pinfeathers; but it is better to have ducks with pinfeathers than no ducks at all.

No complaints have been brought to my attention, although for some years I was actively associated with the fish and game protective association in New Brunswick. I am not in the habit of congratulating the minister or other members of the government on what they do, and in that respect I differ from some of the members on this side of the house. At the same time I would say to the minister that I believe he has taken a step in the right direction in shortening the season and limiting the bag for our water-fowl. I think it is clear that the waterfowl, despite all conservation measures that have been taken, are decreasing in this country and the situation has to be faced. This may be due partly to the drought, but it is due largely to overshooting, and if it is due to overshooting in the last year or two, when so 
many of our men have been overseas, what will the condition be like in the next few years unless something is done? It would be a great calamity if these birds were wiped out or further reduced in numbers. The only suggestion I have to make is that the minister would be well advised to consult, as no doubt he does consult, Mr. Tufts, the migratory birds officer of the maritime provinces, who is familiar with these matters and who, I know, is very much interested in the conservation of such birds.

The hon. member for Westmorland and the hon. member for Cumberland have already seen me with regard to the matter. Apparently there is a peculiar situation in that district, differing from that in other parts of the eastern coast. I have been receiving communications. The hon. member for Cumberland has asked me to give the matter my personal attention and I shall do so. I understand that some communications have come in which I have not been able to see to-day, but I will look into the matter and, if possible, try to rectify it.

I thank the minister. As far as Mr. Tufts is concerned, I know he has done excellent work and his intentions are good. But he lives in a part of the province where the season opens two or three weeks earlier than it does in the area about which the hon. member for Westmorland and I have been speaking, and it also closes later. So that if the season opened two weeks earlier in the Chignecto area it would be comparable to the season in the district in which Mr. Tufts himself lives. Again I wish to say I appreciate the splendid work which Mr. Tufts has done in protecting the bird life of this country.

I do not think the migratory birds officer of the maritime provinces will be influenced by the particular district in which he lives. Knowing him as I do, I think what is going to influence him is his interest in the conservation of these birds. That will be his first and fundamental interest, and it is on that principle that he will base his judgment.

This is a particularly important item in that it has to do with the responsibility of the Canadian people toward
130,000	or so of our red brothers who live among us. These people have hopes, fears, and ambitions just as we have. The vast majority of them, when you go among them to study their conditions, are found to be severely subjected and frustrated in their efforts to do anything. They are badly exploited and greatly misunderstood in Canada. They are often blamed for many things of which they are not guilty. Our responsibility should go to the extent of training these people, informing them and maintaining them under a proper standard of living, giving them an opportunity to make that contribution to Canadian life of which they are capable. Some of the worst features of the whole situation are found to be that under the administration to-day the Indian himself has no appeal, no voice in his own affairs, no way of making his difficulties and trials heard, and he lives in a state of abject subjugation. The result is disease, want and suffering among these people, such as should not prevail in Canada, and it goes even to the extent of ill treatment.
In making a study of conditions among the Indians, and the principles under which we operate this department, I find that there are certain treaties signed by those people who, years ago, took over this Canada of ours from the Indians. They signed treaties with various Indians in different parts of the dominion. If you study these treaties signed by representatives of Queen Victoria and other sovereigns you will find how the government of to-day lives up to them. You find such flagrant violations of the treaties as to give us pause. You find also that those officials who were put in charge of the Indians have in
many cases dictatorial power and complete control over the life and existence of these people. The training of the Indian is incomplete. There is no real opportunity for him such as there is for the whites, and one is sometimes astounded at the apathy of Canadians generally to the conditions among these people. They are put off on reserves in sparsely settled areas.
They can fish in British Columbia just as well as the white man.

I know the hon. member is capable of giving us his opinion and I have no doubt he will do so, but there are
130,000	Indians and they are not all fishing salmon in British Columbia. They have no place to which to appeal to obtain redress for their conditions; there is no one in authority to speak for them; they have no voice. They have not the capacity properly to organize themselves. These people have character and ability. They have a fine attitude toward one another and toward life generally. When we have conscripted them into the army or when they have volunteered they have made good soldiers. They can be a great people; they have proved that when they have been able to escape from the control of the department. Many things remain to be done to make them economically sound. First of all, they can make a living. Where they have had an opportunity they have proved themselves to be good.
I am not going to deal with the troubles of the past or the record of Canada in the past in the treatment of these fine people. I am looking forward to what we can do toward salvaging them and helping them to make their contribution to Canada, and they can make a great contribution. Toward this end I think this year has marked a step forward. The minister in charge of the department is to be congratulated on the fact that, he has some new officials who seem to have a vision of what is needed. After some years of protest,
[DOT] a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate was finally set up to make a study of this problem. It was not a royal commission as we had hoped. I was disappointed that, after the committee met, it did not see fit to invite Indians to send representatives who could sit on the committee and give us some evidence of actual conditions of life on the reserve and what opportunities they have. After all, people living on these reserves under the Indian agents and under the control as they have it to-day could give us the best information. As proof of my contention that the Indians can give us the best information, on August 6 last we had before-

us an Indian. His story is of great interest and should be an eye-opener to the Canadian people. This Indian has gone so far and -has made such a success of his life because twenty-five years ago he made up his mind to escape from the Indian reserve and controls. He made a living for himself. He joined the army in the two wars and rose to the highly important position of being a brigadier in the Canadian army. They should be on
the record here; the members of this committee should have them. He told how his father started out on the Indian reserve at Brantford. His father was a carpenter, an industrious man who worked his way up. He obtained some contracts and worked in the Indian department on his own reserve. He said:
Therefore whenever he was awarded a contract, it was necessary for him to make an arrangement with a Brantford city merchant, through the Indian agent, to supply him with materials and cash for his work, to be paid back when the cheque came through, as it eventually did, in payment for the completed job.
He was talking about building a bridge on the reserve. He said:
During the summer of 1911 or 1912 he got a larger contract than usual, for building a reinforced concrete bridge which took some two or three months to complete. In due course the work was done. The cheque came along. The accounting was made with the merchant showing that my father had a balance due him of $1,600. The cheque was endorsed, and when he called for his money a day or so later, he was given $1,100 only, with the explanation from the agent that somewhere a mistake had been made. When he demanded to be shown where the mistake was he was put off. time after time, and never was shown to the time of his death. To get contracts, you have to do what is commonly known as "play ball" with the Indian agents. In those days, although the council of the Six Nations awarded the contract, the agent had to approve and recommend it to the then department before it was finally granted by them. I am not at this late date accusing the agent of theft. I intend only to show how some agents disregard the obligations which they should have towards the people they are expected to instruct and guide.
Then he goes on to show how he was denied an education, and although the Six Nations themselves passed resolutions asking the sovemment to grant money for the education of these men, it was turned down. He went to the department and asked why they turned down the request of the Six Nations Indians

themselves to spend some of their own money in educating these men. He was surprised to get their answer which was as follows:
It is no use sending you Indians to school, you just go back to the reserve anyway.
He served in the army, went back to the reserve, got some education and started teaching school there. He got some land under the soldier settlement board of the first great war and found that he would not be allowed to rent this land and continue with his work of teaching, in spite of the fact that he had been given the assurance that he would be allowed to do so. He found that his job was taken away from him. He then proceeded to tell the story of his whole life. Finally, in despair he became so angered at the Indian agent-he was so badly treated-that he decided to get away. This man was particularly anxious that the department should do something about their conduct toward the Indians in order to remove the antagonism which existed amongst many of the old people toward the administration.
There is also the efforts of the Indians themselves. Another representative of the Indians was a man by the name of Andrew Paul, who is the chairman or president of some North American Indian brotherhood. He appeared before the committee. He was chosen by the Indians to protest against the way they have been treated. Probably the North American Indian brotherhood was not constitutionally organized. There are difficulties in their organization, but it was the best the Indians could do. I do not think he himself had done very much in the way of preparing his work, and his evidence before the committee was not as good as that of the brigadier. At any rate it showed the efforts of the Indians themselves to get redress for their wrongs.
Generally speaking, the committee has done a great deal of good. It has done a great deal toward focusing attention on a serious problem in Canada. It has revealed serious conditions and has given a great deal of hope to these frustrated people. It has given facts and figures which should be of great help to hon. members in dealing with the problem of how the Canadian people are ,to treat their red brothers.
The committee soon realized what a great job there was to be done, particularly when they started to investigate some of the treaties and the problems of the Indians as a whole as they exist from coast to coast among the different Indians. That was particularly true of some of the Indians in certain areas who are not so well advanced or so well able to take care of themselves, or are so progressively

tions across the whole country are to be studied, at least two years more work will have to be done. I am sure that the minister will have the support of all members of that committee and most members in the house in carrying on that work.
There are a number of things which the Indian organizations across Canada have demanded in connection with the Indian Act which this committee is studying. It was asked that a commission be set up to get actual data on conditions, and they were emphatic that there should be Indian representation on that committee, that there should be a complete revision and study of the Indian treaties and that the federal government should be asked to take care of Indians seventy years of age and over in the same way that their white brothers are cared for.
They also requested that the Indian Act be so amended that no decision affecting the welfare of the Indians could be made without the consent of the Indian band. This would cover such matters as membership in the band, training and so on. They asked for properly equipped and staffed day schools and that assistance be granted to indigent, ill and disabled Indians. They asked also that steps be taken immediately to improve the terrible health conditions that exist across Canada.
I think the committee will approve the general steps taken by the department. The Indians are only too anxious to do what they can in bringing about a greater assimilation. They want to work along with their white brothers. All they are asking is a fair deal, the right to the pursuit of happiness, the right to make a living for themselves and the right to make the contribution of which they are capable. There is a new hope among these Indians and it is up to us to see that those hopes are not frustrated.

I doubt if I would have been making this speech had it not been that one morning I looked out of my office window and saw a delegation of Indians coming up to the House of Commons. I was interested enough to visit the railway committee room and listen in for a time on the interviews. I am not going to repeat the doleful song of the hon. member for Yorkton. He has lived up to his record in connection with this subject as well as with others. I am going to tell a bright story about the Indians.
I was elected in the spring of 1937 and I commenced getting complaints from around my riding. I got complaints from the Indian reserve at Golden Lake. I visited that reserve on a number of occasions and found that

Supply-Indian Affairs

conditions were not too happy. I went to the department and made some suggestions. These Indians are located on poor land, but I suggested that this land be torn up even if the department had to purchase a tractor and other mechanized equipment to do this. After I listened to the proceedings in the railway committee room and heard some of the complaints made about the treatment of Indians in Canada, I took occasion to run up one evening to this reserve. Although it was a hurried trip, I was able to pick up a few things which were quite enlightening as to what can be accomplished by the Indians in the way of helping themselves.
I understand it was a Mr. Morris in the department who was largely responsible for what has been done there. The department did not accept my suggestion about buying a tractor but they did buy some good horses. These were not little, scrubby horses that were not able to pull a wheelbarrow; they were well-matched teams with proper harness. These horses were put in the hands of a man who knew how to handle them, who knew how to care for them, who knew how to shoe them, who knew how to keep their harness in good shape. The department paid this man a moderate sum per month to take care of these horses and the chickens and hogs that they had.
The result was that before very long they were able to tear up a few acres here and a few acres a mile or so away. They picked out the best land and they went to work in a cooperative way. We hear talk about Indian agents who are dictators, but the agent there is just the opposite. This man would not think of saying a cross word to an Indian. When they go to plant potatoes he does not stand around and watch the men and women do the work; he picks up a pail and goes along with them. The result of all this has been that, instead of importing almost 100 per cent of the food they need, they are practically self-supporting. A marvellous transformation has taken place in that reserve.
They built a community pit. During the season the Indians come to the pit once a week, and the Indian agent is there to hand them out their allotment of the different vegetables that have been grown. They can grow anything at all. The land is poor, but there is plenty of it and it is no poorer than other land that has raised large families. They get their supplies of vegetables from the community pit. There is one thing about our Indians; they will not take any more than they require.

Then they began to bring in day-old chicks. These chicks are kept until they are large enough to be shipped to other reserves, even as far away as the one at Moosonee. This means that Indians on these outlying reserves now have hens. Indians who never before tasted hens' eggs now have their own little flock of hens around their doors, and their own eggs. They raise their own hogs and keep a number of brood sows. These hogs are distributed among the Indians as they require them.
In the earlier days, when one would drive through that reserve, he would never see a supply of wood in front of an Indian's home, although he might see a few green poles. When I was up there this summer I saw in front of every home a large pile of dry wood. They get together and cut their wood, and by working together, sawing it and splitting it, they have a plentiful supply of dry wood for the winter months, rather than a hand-to-mouth supply of green wood.
After they have shipped their pullets to the outlying reserves, the roosters are left to handle. The hon. member for Yorkton has talked about the government taking care of the aged and the ill. But the Indians in the reserve in Renfrew North are not asking anyone to take care of their aged or ill. They keep those roosters until the weather gets cold. Then they kill and freeze them, and after they are stored they are ready to be handed out to the aged and the ill.
They ask no one to take care of their sick. They work cooperatively and take turns sitting with any sick persons night after night. They have organized a homemakers' club. A lady named Mrs. LaValle, who, I believe, is one of the finest citizens to be found in any county, has taken responsibility in this matter. Through the operations of the homemakers' club the clothing is sent to the Indian reserve. Mrs. LaValle, as president, gets the ladies together, and any clothing that is sent in is transformed into clothing for the children. In this way they are warmly clothed and well clad, without any great effort on the part of anyone.
Then, in these years of transformation numerous new homes have been going up. Instead of being content to live in shacks, many of the Indians are building themselves fine homes. These are not too expensive, because they cut the timber on the reserve, take it to the sawmill to have it sawed, and do the building operations themselves. The result is that they are building good homes.
It is interesting to point out that the Indians in this reserve went up the river and there secured a discarded lumber camp. They had

Supply-Indian Affairs
to cut it in two to get it across the railway tracks; but, after considerable difficulty, they brought it down the river, with the result that, when I was there, they were just putting the finishing touches on a fine community hall, and that right in the Indian reserve.
A new industry is being established on that reserve in the form of a sawmill and planing mill. One of the regulations is that Indians on the reserve get a preference in the matter of labour.
Perhaps one of the most interesting advances made by those Indians is that they have gone in for the raising of goats. They developed breeding stock, although not so much for themselves, because they have a supply of milk from the dairies, if they want to avail themselves of it. However, they are raising goats and shipping them to all the reserves across Canada. Indeed, some of them may reach the Indians in Yorkton constituency. These goats are taken, at times, by the nomad Indians who get into their boats in the spring of the year, camping here and there as they choose. They will tie the legs of a goat and put it into a boat. As they proceed, the goat finds no difficulty in securing fodder, and in return the Indians have a supply of milk.
We hear much complaint about tuberculosis among the Indians, and I have no reason to doubt the reports. We were troubled with it in the Renfrew North reserve. I believe there were half a dozen cases among the Indians in that reserve, but when they started to keep goats there were no new cases reported. It seems to me that is proof-and I am sure there is other proof available-that goats' milk is at least a preventive of tuberculosis.
Large quantities of hay are required to feed their goats. They do not depend altogether on what they can grow on their reserve. If they have not enough there they go out into the neighbouring country and buy the hay as it stands. With their mowing machines, their wagons and horses they cut the hay, buy it at a moderate price and bring it to the reserve. In this way they save possibly $400 or $500 in a year.
One-fifth of the population of that reserve entered the armed forces and made a fine record for themselves. That is a most creditable showing.
The hon. member for Yorkton referred to training. Let me tell him that the training on the reserve in Renfrew North is becoming inadequate, owing to the fact that they are so anxious to go to school and to keep their children at school. The result has been that they have to build a new schoolhouse this year, or double the present accommodation and add a new teacher.

If the hon. member for Yorkton were to ask one of the officials in the department I think he would be told that, prior to the transformation I have been talking about, that reserve was one of the worst spots in Canada. I was very much interested to hear the fine report of the hon. member for Renfrew North on the reserves he has visited. I think it proves several things, one being that given a chance, Indians are people and capable of improving their own conditions if they are given intelligent leadership. That is all that we in this group have ever asked for the Indians, that we remove the stigma of colour, just as we ask that the colour stigma be removed from the black man because his skin is black, or from the Chinese because his skin is yellow, or that the stigma be removed from woman just because she is born a female. We recognize that these are people and that, as people, they have basic human rights.
It is interesting to know that' the family allowance has had a reflection in better school attendance. If we gave the Indians the old age pension, more of them might live to be seventy. I do not think the hon. member's idea of old age security agrees with mine. If all I get when I get to be seventy is some frozen roosters, I do not want to live to be seventy, and I want chicken before I am

seventy. The roosters are a good thing for children and middle-aged people too. Again I do not think they are old age security.
When I get to be seventy I should like some chicken soup.

I hope the hon. member will be on a reserve too if old age pensions are still withheld from the Indians. It is a shame and disgrace that we should withhold the old age pension from any Canadian, most of all from the first and original Canadians in this country who should have first claim on it. I am reminded of the story I heard not long ago of an Indian who was taken to Hollywood and, after he was shown its wonders, the director said to him, "How do you like our lay-out?". The Indian replied, "How do you like our country?" Some of us seem to forget that this land was the original birthright of the Indian. We have taken from him all but the poorest land, and we insist that dozens of Indian families live on a very small acreage that no white man would attempt to use as a basis for a family farm. I have many Indians in my constituency. I not only visit them but I visit the Indians across the river in the constituency of the Minister of Agriculture, and they are not any better off than mine, because too many Indian families are trying to exist on a very small and poor hilly valley where the arable land is extremely limited and the equipment very poor. A white man would not attempt to live in a community where one biiyier was shared with forty families.
I was interested in what the hon. member said about horses. I like horses too and I should expect the Indians would, but I would hate to have to share a team of horses with thirty families, because none of us would have the use of the horses for a sufficient number of days to be of any use.
I think our whole approach to this problem is wrong, but any time that I hear of an experiment which has succeeded I am glad of it. I hope we shall have a change of attitude and regard these people as capable of intelligence and integrity and that we shall give them a chance to exercise it.
I had the pleasure of listening to Brigadier Martin over the air last week. He made an excellent speech and said the very same things that the hon. member for Yorkton has said. He said this too, "We do not expect to turn into white men but we are capable of becoming good Indians." I think truer words were never spoken. I wish the minister would see fit to put education into the hands of the province because, by keeping it under the jurisdiction of the federal government, you rob

yourself of the best educators in every province. The teachers now are organized. They pay into a superannuation fund and at a certain age they enjoy retirement and superannuation benefits. But if they go to teach in an Indian school they lose those years and get no credit for them, so that the good teachers will not teach on your reserves, because that destroys their superannuation continuity and means that they lose so many years out of their teaching life. I think we might well make an arrangement with the provinces whereby we would spend the money we now spend on education, in grants-in-aid on a per capita basis, and put into the hands of the provincial governments the administration of education not only for white children but for Indian children. I think we would have new standards of education in our schools and there would be more people like Brigadier Martin coming out of them, individuals in a position to give capable leadership to their own people. Brigadier Martin is an example of the sort of thing that happens when you expose intelligence to the process of education. We should have several of Brigadier Martin's kind in this house representing the Indian people. I hope the day is not far distant when Indians will elect Indians to speak for them and represent them in this house as they now do in New Zealand-where four Maoris sit in the New Zealand house and one of them is always in the cabinet because of a statutory provision to that effect. Sometimes the Maori has sat in the cabinet without portfolio, but one of the best ministers of health that New Zealand has ever produced was a Maori. I think people of the calibre of Brigadier Martin could very well sit in this house with members like you and me.

I understand that the only dental care the Indians are allowed is to have a tooth extracted; there is no dental treatment given. I think that is why so many Indian children and adults, when they reach twenty or twenty-five years of age have no teeth at all.

I did not ask that this item be held over in order that I might make comments upon it. I asked rather that it should stand over in order that I might ask the minister to explain, in not too elaborate detail, the administration of the lumber resources of some of these national parks, and what the government is doing to prevent flood damage arising from streams running out of these parks. In order to let the committee and the minister understand my problem, let me say this:
When the three prairie provinces became provinces, forty-one years ago, in 1905, their resources were retained by the dominion government. In 1930, I think it was, the resources were returned to the provinces, and for the last sixteen years have been under provincial jurisdiction. In the province of Manitoba one section of these resources, the land area now called the Riding Mountain national park, was turned over to the administration of the dominion government for the purpose of making it a national park. The resources, including this park, are now owned by the province. But this park is completely turned over for administrative purposes to the dominion, on an undertaking by the dominion that it would establish there and maintain a national park. I suppose it is from ten to thirty miles wide and perhaps 100 miles or more long: these are not the exact boundaries but approximately. This park is an elevated section of the province in the western central part of southern Manitoba. The ground is undulating and covered with trees. Because of its elevation, it is subject to late

spring and, early fall frosts. This combination of conditions prompted the government to make it first into a forest reserve and now into a national park.
The people adjoining the area are interested in two things, among others. They are interested in getting some of the surplus lumber from the park for purposes of build-and construction and bridge construction and so on. I want to ask the minister what the government's policy-perhaps his policy is the same for the other parks-is with respect to making the lumber in that park available, because now the people adjoining the area find it difficult to get lumber at all, and if they can get it from the park, and if they can get it in rather larger quantities than before, a good community service will have been rendered.	_ _
The other point I want to ask the minister about is this. Because of the large extent of that area, and because it is elevated, perhaps about twice as high above sea level as the ordinary farm lands of Manitoba, and because during the last half century some of the trees have been removed and the beavers have nearly all been destroyed-beavers which built dams that held back the streams-the result now is that in the spring the waters rush down the streams rapidly, carrying silt and filling up the ditches in the farming communities below and causing serious flood damage. The farmers in the municipalities just out from the foothills of these mountains have not only had that added burden put upon them; but, as a result of these floods, their crops have in some years been partly and in other years largely destroyed. It is possible the minister may have outlined his policy on these matters when I was not here, and I do not want him to take up time in repeating what he may have already said with respect to the preservation of timber and making it available to the people adjoining the reserves. But I should like to know what the government is doing to avoid the recurring damage year after year from these mountain streams which rush down carrying silt and filling the ditches which the people have gone to great expense to dig, thus delaying the time of seeding and often damaging and sometimes destroying the growing crops.
To bring the matter more specifically to the minister's attention, here is a typical request from a municipality with reference to lumber. I quote:
Owing to the scarcity of lumber it is impossible to repair municipal bridges as well as necessary repairs to other buildings, therefore we request that the amount of lumber allowed on timber limits in the Riding Mountain national park be increased and also that the area where cutting is permitted be enlarged.

This is typical of the problems of the farmers and the requests from those out on the farm land below the mountains. This is the area where their crops, for forty years to my knowledge, have been frequently damaged because of surplus water running from this elevated section of country. I quote again from one of these representations from municipalities with respect to flood damage:
Our main trouble is the drainage maintenance. As you know, spring thaw and heavy June rains rush down from Riding Mountain carrying silt and depositing it on the low land, filling ditches, which means we have to be continually dredging. The cost is more than the municipality can bear.

The leader of the opposition has asked me two questions, one with regard to the permits for cutting timber. The practice in the Riding Mountain park is this. A survey was made by officers of all timber in the park, and that survey shows what was old and what was new, what could be cut and what should be left. That survey is in the' hands of the superintendent of the park; all permits that are issued are issued only for that portion of the forest which can be cut, and it is given to those in the immediate neighbourhood. When the hon. member speaks of preserving the parks, one of the greatest means of preservation is, of course, the timber in it, and therefore it is strictly looked after to see that the park is not denuded of that which makes it so beautiful in itself. Permits are given to those in the surrounding areas who are able to go and get their lumber. That is the policy of the department.
With regard to the flow and control of water from Riding Mountain, the hon. member for Dauphin has also been communicating with me, interested through the municipalities adjoining, who are suffering in consequence. It has been the subject of investigation by the engineers of the department, and the province of Manitoba is extremely interested also, with the result that the premier of that province, Mr. Garson, communicated with me,
indicating what was happening and expressing the hope that something might be done as a joint effort between ourselves and the province. I had a letter from Mr. Garson on July 5, in which he makes this statement:
My suggestion would be that the P.F.R.A. be requested to proceed with the construction of the proposed reservoirs and experimental check dams in accordance with the recommendations contained in the report of December 13, 1945; that your department provide the necessary dumping grounds as recommended in the report (which lands may subsequently be included within the boundaries of the Riding Mountain park); and that the province, in conjunction with interested municipalities, undertake the work of rehabilitating existing ditches as well as providing such additional ditches as may be required to carry the face water from the dumping grounds to a proper outlet. If you agree with the general suggestions contained in the preceding paragraph, I would further suggest that an early joint dominion-provincial survey be undertaken at the earliest possible date.
We had our officers in before this matter had been brought up by t.he hon. member for Dauphin or the leader of the opposition and they were making a survey, but on receipt of Premier Garson's letter we have now sent an officer with instructions to make a survey of the park and to advise as to what should be done to remedy the condition now existing. He will get in contact with the officials of the province of Manitoba, and together they may make recommendations for alleviating and controlling the waters that are flowing down and damaging surrounding farm property. That, report, I hope, we shall receive very soon. I wish to have it clearly understood that I am just as anxious to have that done as the hon. member for Dauphin or the leader of the opposition. I hope I shall have the report shortly and, in conjunction with the province, have something done to rectify what is certainly a grave difficulty in the way of farming around that country.

However, I rose to remind him and the government that immigration in this country is still a front-page topic and will remain so until such time as we do something definite about it. There are no groups, or no organization or representative bodies, in fact very few individuals in this country, who do not think we need more people. We need them now. I do not suggest that the government is unmindful of the situation, but it is the government's responsibility to arrange the how and how many. The committee is well aware that

Supply-Immigration
the number of emigrants in Europe is not unlimited. In the main, those who survived were young people. These young people are needed by their own countries not only to rebuild but to repopulate them. At the present time we are merely nibbling at the problem, while other countries are stealing a march on us. Australia is up to her neck in emigrants from the British isles and Scandinavian countries. They have already made provision for some 70,000 this year, and 50,000 war orphans over a period of three years. Brazil is in the field for 250,000 from continental Europe, and so is the Argentine. I merely bring these facts to the attention of the committee to indicate that there is some hurry about this matter, because the best will likely be picked over.
Here we have a country with unlimited reserves and great potentialities, with an abundance of international good will, and yet for all purposes we are a land without people. It is well to realize that the first wave of immigrants who came to this country was for the expansive development of the country and entirely in the field of agricultural economy. It was an introduction of the people to the land and the land to the people. We are now ready for another wave, a second wave of immigrants for the intensive development of our resources, for the use of the country by the people and in order to be able to consolidate the industrial position which we now occupy as a result of the tremendous and agreeable job which we did during the war. Pessimists notwithstanding, I point out that there is a shortage and there will continue to be a shortage of construction workers, miners, people for the forests, agriculturists, domestics, and in almost any other walk of life in the country.
There is one aspect of this whole problem that we sometimes ignore, namely, the problem of emigration. As the committee well knows, we are suffering some cruel losses to the United States at the rate of 30,000 this year. This 30,000 is draining away our young and our trained. It is well for the committee to recall that from 1900 to 1945 some 5,000,000 immigrants came to this country. At the same time 3,500.000 left. An infinitesimal number went back to their own country; in the main the rest went to the United States. We seem to be a nation that is truly looking south for greater opportunities for recognition of our capabilities and for a larger material compensation. Too long we have been a feeder and1 a half-way house to the United States. We have, our country here to build up. Our destiny is to be the front door to the world rather than the back door to another nation. We have to make Canada more attractive. We 63260-346
have to replace those whom we have lost. It is necessary that we consolidate our industrial market; we should increase our home markets and we should populate our unpopulated areas. We have established ourselves as the first of the middle powers, and we should try to hold that position.

I did intend to make a statement, but the hon. member for Spadina got ahead of me. I may be a little longer than eleven o'clock and I hope I shall be able to finish my statement. As the committee knows, the present regulations and law concerning immigration are quite clear and they have been referred to already this session. In addition to British subjects and United States citizens, the present regulations provide for the admission of, first, the wife or unmarried child under eighteen years of age of any person legally admitted to Canada who has sufficient means to maintain himself until employment is secured; second, an agriculturist having sufficient means to farm in Canada; third, the fiancee of an adult male legally admitted to and resident in Canada, who is in a position to receive, marry and care for his intended wife; fourth, a person, who, having entered Canada as a non-immigrant, enlisted in the Canadian armed forces and, having served in such forces, has been honourably discharged therefrom.
Alien immigrants other than United States citizens require to be in possession of a properly vised passport, but by the order in council which I tabled on May 28 last, the door was opened and the following were admitted:
The father or mother, the unmarried son or daughter eighteen years of age or over, the unmarried brother or sister, the orphan nephew or niece under sixteen years of age, of any person legally admitted to and resident in Canada who is in a position to receive and care for such relative. The term "orphan" means a child bereaved of both parents.
Then there was a provision made with regard to passports. These people could not obtain passports because they were stateless persons, and it was provided that it would be sufficient to have a travel document establishing the identity of the holder in the case of an immigrant who had been displaced from his country of origin as a result of the war and who was not in possession of a valid passport. That is the way we have it to-day. It was thought at the time that that extension was warranted, and I thought so too. But the first thing dealt with after the war was the transportation of our forces and their dependents from overseas, and it was felt that they should have a priority over others. That was done.
I recall to the committee, too, that during the war we had, I believe, about 4,000 refugees who came from Great Britain and other countries, and ultimately we gave them permanent landing. These persons, while here, proved to be very good citizens, and many of them had given a fine contribution to our

The reason was that we were making an effort to take in soldiers who would go on the land, and into agricultural pursuits. We had many requests, and there was quite an agitation with regard to the Polish soldiers. They had expressed their intention most freely, that they were not going back to Poland, and that they intended to look elsewhere. Canada was one of the places to which they would go.

How many still remain?

Twelve thousand dependents, but my officials cannot tell me how many soldiers. But our first duty, of course, was to see that our soldiers were returned, as well as their dependents.
Now, with the passage of time, the numbers are decreasing. The soldiers are being brought here and rehabilitating themselves in the country. The numbers are lessening as the days go by.
There was another vexed question, namely the question of fiancees. Many of our young men are to-day anxious to have their fiancees come here. But priority was given first to the wives and children, rather than to the fiancees.
The whole question resolved itself into one of transportation. One hon. member 63260-346J
spoke about the numbers in England who wanted to come. There is nothing to prevent their going to our office in London, being examined there and settlement conditions investigated in connection with coming to Canada, with the exception of that one thing, namely that they could not get transportation. This problem will always come up when we are dealing with this matter. The hon. member for Spadina mentioned shipping from the continent. There has been an indication given that the Scandinavian line are going to send some vessels, and also the Hol-land-American line. But these may convey only a very few of those who are on the continent now. We have there about 2,000 dependents and about 2,000 fiancees, and, in addition, there are 1,000 dependents of residents of Canada to be repatriated. They were there all during the war, are still there, and have no transportation.
Therefore, owing to this extreme shortage of vessels, I have had to say to all those who are asking to come to this country, "How are we going to do it? We have no method by which we, as a department, can give priority to anyone sailing to this country." They must, of themselves, find that sailing. But when it came to the question of an individual who was not a dependent and not a soldier, that person simply could not get passage in preference to those, and none of us would have wished to encourage them in the slightest degree.
On the other question with regard to the opening of the door for these other people in Europe, they were exactly in the same position. Some of them may have relatives in this country. Transportation in Europe today is in chaos; there is no method by which they can be transferred from one country to another in the manner in which they could prior to the war. There is the difficulty in connection with the exchanges between countries; there is the difficulty of travelling in any one country.
The question came up then, of course, with regard to our medical facilities which must be on hand before we can deal with these. We are in a position now whereby, if we can get accommodation on the continent with respect to offices, we can staff those offices and deal with them. We have, of course, to have the consent of the countries through which these immigrants must pass. At the present time we are reopening the Paris office and also the office at The Hague. Perhaps in Antwerp there may be some chance later, of also establishing an office there. So far as the Scandinavian countries are concerned, the only method by which it can be done is by sending

officers there in order to investigate those who desire to come. At the present time the * Department of External Affairs is dealing with the countries involved. I shall not be long. I should like to proceed, so that hon. members may have it on the record and discuss it to-morrow.
Then, repeatedly we have been asked throughout the country to formulate a policy. It has been suggested that that policy should be a large one, and one would think that it must be done overnight. The government is fully alive to the seriousness and magnitude of the immigration policy. I believe that the country generally is fully aware of that. When it is suggested in an editorial that there should be selective immigration, and in the next breath that there should be no discrimination, then I venture to say to those who are making the suggestions that I do not see how we can have selective immigration without discrimination. I should like to have the answer to that, because there have been many editorials. I have no complaints against them. I wish to have as many opinions as there are in order that a worthwhile policy may be evolved. The government is thoroughly seized of the fact that an immigration policy must necessarily be stated sooner or later, and a subcommittee of the cabinet has been formed. We have had that subcommittee established for some months, as well as an inter-departmental committee of high-ranking officers who have been engaged in studying different questions dealing with immigration, and who will of course, give us the benefit- of their advice. That concerns domestic policy.
Then we have the refugee question. That is not purely Canadian; it is international in scope. We have a representative on the united nations organization which will be meeting in September. At that meeting consideration will

be given to the question of refugees and the stateless persons of Europe, and as one of the united nations Canada will, I presume, be asked to take her share of these stateless persons and will have to assume her obligations as a member of the united nations. So that we are dealing with the matter as best we can. Anyone coming within the admissible classes who goes to our offices in England and passes the medical inspection can come here, provided that settlement conditions in this country are satisfactory and provided that they can get transportation.
I do not think there is anything I can add except that I hope in the near future we shall have some word with regard to the setting up of our offices in Europe and some idea of what we may plan in the way of government policy.
